pages.body:
# Dashboard

The Dashboard is a management area that gathers production indicators in one place. It is visible in company-wide mode and reserved for managers and admins.

::: info Early preview
The Dashboard is in early preview. New charts and indicators will be added over time.
:::

## How to open it

In the left menu, switch to company-wide mode and click **Dashboard** at the top of the list.

## Charts

### Assemblies marked ready — weekly

A line chart that shows how many panels each production line marked as ready, week by week, over the last 12 weeks.

- One line per production line.
- One mark per ISO week (Monday-based).
- Lines with no ready events in the period are not shown.

Use this chart to compare throughput between lines, spot drops or peaks, and check whether weekly production is keeping a steady pace.

pages.title: Production Lines
pages.body:
# Production Lines

A company must have at least one production line defined in the system.

Production Settings is a menu group with three views. **Production lines** holds the lines and their stations. **Machine settings** holds the machine setups. **Automations** holds the action triggers and the setups they run: machine files and drawings.

File generation templates are not here — they live in **File settings**, under the Files section of the menu. See [Reports](/guide/reports/).

## The Production lines view

Each production line is a row: a header with its name, what it builds, its counts and its actions, and below it the cards of its stations in the order the line runs them.

Rows can be collapsed with the arrow on the left. They all start open, and the ones you collapse stay collapsed the next time you open the view.

Lines are grouped by what they build: modules first, then assemblies, then parts. A line that builds more than one of these appears once, under the largest one. Lines with an unrecognised tipo go to a last group, *Other*.

**Machine settings** are grouped by machine type. Licensed types show how many setups you have out of your licensed maximum. Each card lists what uses the setup — stations and production lines alike — and warns only when nothing does.

### Working with stations

At the end of every line there are two tiles:

- **New Production Station** creates a station and adds it to that line.
- **Add existing station** lists every station that is not already in the line, including the ones with no line at all.

**Reordering** is done by dragging a station card by its handle. The new order is saved as soon as you drop the card. You cannot drag a card from one line into another: to move a station, add it to the new line and then remove it from the old one.

A station can belong to **several lines** at once. It then gets a card in each of them, marked **SHARED**, and its cards list the lines it is in. It is the same station in all of them, so editing it from any line changes it everywhere. Its position, on the other hand, belongs to each line separately.

Stations that belong to **no line** are listed at the end of the view, under *No production line*. This is normal — a station can be created or left without a line — and it is the only place where you can reach them.

**Deleting a station** asks what you mean:

- *Remove from this line* takes it out of that line only. The station stays, and if it was in no other line it moves to the *No production line* group.
- *Delete* removes the station from every line and loses its checklist. This cannot be undone.

### The machine of a line

A line can name the machine it runs on. Tick **Line machine** in the line form and pick one.

There are two ways to record it, and both are fine:

- **On the line.** Use this when the line *is* one machine — a saw line, a plates cutter. There are no stations to hang it on.
- **On a single station.** Use this when the line has one station and the machine belongs to it. Nothing changes for the lines you already set up this way.

Either way, the machine's name appears on the line header, next to what the line builds. When it was read off a station rather than set on the line, it is shown in grey italics, so you can tell at a glance where it came from.

If a line has a machine **and** one of its stations has another one, the form says so. The line's machine is the one that counts for the line. It is a notice, not an error: the form saves either way.

A line with several stations that each have their own machine — an automated panel line — has no single machine to name. Give it one by creating a **MOB2 production line** machine setup and picking it as the line machine. That setup exists to hold what belongs to the whole line rather than to one of its tables; it has no settings yet, and each one will appear as it starts being used.

### Picking a machine setup

Both machine pickers — the one on a station and the one on a line — put the setups that usually go there first, and everything else under **Other machines**. Nothing is hidden: if you pick a setup from the second group, the form tells you where it normally goes and lets you carry on.

When you create a machine setup, the **Model** list is grouped the same way, by where that kind of machine goes:

- **Production line settings** — holds what belongs to a whole line. Today that is *H&M MOB2 production line*.
- **Machine stations** — goes on a station of a line.
- **Standalone machines** — machines you send generated files to: saws, cutters, profilers. These can also be named as the machine of a logistics line.

Most models have no settings of their own: a cutter is configured by the options of the file it is sent, not by a form here. When that is the case the form says so instead of showing you an empty one.

### The machine configuration file

Some machine models accept the machine's own configuration file (XML or INI). Uploading it fills the **parsed params**, shown next to the uploader as read-only JSON: the top level is open and each block can be expanded. The parsed params include a `parsed` entry with the date and time the file was read, so you always know how old the configuration is.

## Automations

Two things live in this view, and one uses the other: the **setups**, which say *how* something is generated, and the **action triggers**, which say *when*.

### Machine file setups

A machine file setup is a saved MOB v2 setup: how the machine file is built — operations, nailing, shifts and layers.

Running one takes a panel design, builds the machine file for **every station of every production line**, and sends it to the machines. There is no report and no download in between, and there is no way to limit it to a single line.

You use a machine file setup from two places:

- an **action trigger**, so it runs on its own, and
- the **AUTO MOB v2** file type, to run it by hand on the panels you pick.

### Drawing setups

A drawing setup is a saved set of drawings. It decides:

- **Views to generate** — front, top, section, back, bottom, right.
- **One drawing per zone** — an extra drawing per zone of the panel, with the parts of the other zones drawn as a dashed outline.
- **Include the framework (zone 0)** — the woods-only layer, drawn as FRAMEWORK.
- **Positioning origin** — where the parts are placed from.

Running one takes a design and writes the drawings straight into the design's files, marked as generated. There is no report in between.

You use a drawing setup from two places:

- an **action trigger**, so it runs on its own, and
- the **Launch action** button on the designs and multipanel groups tables, to run it by hand. Here the setup is optional: without one you get the default views (front, top, section, plus one per zone).

The design's drawings card shows whether a run is working or failed, and warns when a newer IFC arrived after the drawings were made, marking the outdated ones. **Generate the drawings again** from the same button; **Clean** deletes the generated ones without touching the drawings you uploaded yourself.

### Action triggers

An action trigger runs something on its own when an event happens in production, with nobody clicking anything. It reads as three steps:

1. **When this happens** — the event. Today the only event is a design finishing its analysis.
2. **Only if** — an optional condition on a field of the design (`name`, `tipo`, or a key of its client data), matched as a full word, a prefix, or "contains". Leave it empty and the trigger applies to every design.
3. **Then do this** — the action, and the setup it runs with:
   - *Generate MOB v2 files and send them to the machines*, with a machine file setup.
   - *Generate the drawings of the design*, with a drawing setup — or none, for the default views.

::: warning
A trigger runs for **every** design that matches, each time it finishes its analysis. Use *Only if* to narrow it down before turning one on in a busy project.
:::

The production line (PL) itself has the following fields:

- **Name**: A name to identify the PL.
- **Tipo**: Assembly or module categories that the PL can produce.
- **Client IDs**: An optional list of external identifiers used to link the production line to external systems (e.g. ERP or planning software). Multiple IDs can be added when the line needs to be matched from more than one external source.

![Production Line Form](./pl_form.png)

Production lines (PLs) are expected to have at least 1 station. Stations represent steps in the production process. 

Stations fields:


- **Name**: Simply a name.
- **Clien ID**: Client ID of the station, usually comes from an external application that the client want to link.
- **Zones**: What zones are expected to be produced in this stations. For example add 0 for a typical framing station. If two stations in the same production line share a zone, a warning is shown at the top of the line, naming the duplicated zone and the stations it is in.
- **Machine**: If the station is marked as a "machine station", then you have to define a machine setup that will be linked to this station. For example: A MOBI-ONE station defined in "Machines".


As a last nested item, we have checklist items for each station. This will be entries for the production users to be checked in the production interface ("the viewer").

Checklist fields:

- **Task text**: The text that will be shown to the production user.
- **DOCS**: A feature that allows the company to add documentation specific to the task, such as guidelines, specifications, ...
- **Branches**: If empty, this is ignored. If filled, selected branches will be searched in the constructible, to see if it's needed to be added. The station zones are also considered. If station zones exist, then the branch needs to be present in the station zones. Only then the checklist task is included.
- **Inclusion criteria**: All means all checklist will get this task. 1/n will be added in 1 checklist each n checklists started. 1/n randomized will do the same but at a random pace.

pages.title: Multipanel Groups
pages.body:
# Multipanel Groups

Multipanel Groups let you combine multiple wall panels into a single unit that is processed together through the machine. This is a production-level decision — you create groups inside a batch to tell the machine to feed several panels consecutively as one run.

When a group is **locked**, the entire group is treated as a single logical panel by the report system: Bill of Materials reports use the combined rail length, and machine files (MOB2) are generated as one file for the whole group.

::: info Feature flag
Multipanel Groups must be enabled on your company by a Produuz.it administrator. Once enabled, a configuration card appears in each project's settings and a **Multipanel Groups** tab appears in each batch.
:::

[[toc]]

## Project Configuration

Before creating groups, configure the constraints for each project in **Project Settings → Multipanel Groups**.

| Setting | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| **Min height (mm)** | Minimum panel height allowed in a group. |
| **Min / Max element width (mm)** | Allowed width range for individual panels. |
| **Max transport width (mm)** | The combined width of all panels plus gaps must not exceed this value. This is typically the physical limit of the machine or transport system. |
| **Min / Max element count** | Minimum and maximum number of panels per group. |
| **Default gap (mm)** | Default gap between elements when creating a new group. |

## Creating a Group

Navigate to **Batch → Multipanel Groups** and click **New Group**. The creation dialog walks you through four steps:

1. **Select panels** — choose two or more assemblies from the batch. The selector constrains to consecutive production priorities.
2. **Set gaps** — define the gap between each pair of adjacent panels (in mm).
3. **Validate** — run the 8 validation checks (see below). Each requirement shows a pass/fail badge with a detail message.
4. **Name & confirm** — give the group a name and save. The group is saved with status **valid** (or **invalid** if any checks failed).

## Validation Requirements

All 8 requirements must pass before a group can be locked.

| # | Requirement | What is checked |
|---|-------------|-----------------|
| 1 | **Height equality** | All panels must have the same height; each must meet the project minimum. |
| 2 | **Width range** | Each panel's width must be within the configured [min, max] range. |
| 3 | **Element count** | The number of panels must be within [min_count, max_count]. |
| 4 | **Framing match** | Top and bottom rail profile, material, and finish must be identical across all panels. |
| 5 | **Consecutive sequence** | Panels must be consecutive in the production priority order and all in the same batch. |
| 6 | **Identical zones** | The set of zone branches (e.g., insulation zones, openings) must be the same across all panels. |
| 7 | **Transport width** | Total combined width (sum of panel widths + all gaps) must not exceed the configured maximum. |
| 8 | **Panel-layer operations** | Saw and milling operations on the panel layer must be equal across all elements. |

## Group Status

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `draft` | Newly created, not yet validated. |
| `valid` | All validation checks passed — ready to lock. |
| `invalid` | One or more validation checks failed. |
| `locked` | Locked for production. Reports and machine files treat the group as a single panel. |

## Locking a Group

Once a group has **valid** status, open it in the drawer and click **Lock**. On lock:

- The combined rail length (`sum of element widths + gaps`) is computed and stored.
- The group cannot be edited after this point.
- All reports and machine file generators that include any assembly from this group will treat it as a single combined panel going forward.

## Report Form — Assembly Selector

When building a report (BoM, machine files, etc.), the assembly selector is aware of multipanel groups:

- Each assembly that belongs to a group shows a **chip** with the group name and the panel count (e.g. `Group A · 3 panels`). This makes it easy to spot which assemblies are part of a combined unit.
- A **"Force multipanel selection"** toggle is available on the selector. When enabled, selecting any assembly in a group automatically adds all other assemblies of the same group to the selection. This prevents accidentally generating a report for only part of a locked group.

## Bill of Materials Impact

When generating a BoM report (Wood BoM, Plates BoM, etc.) that includes assemblies belonging to a **locked** Multipanel Group:

- The top rail and bottom rail parts are replaced by a single virtual part spanning the full group width.
- The rail **length** in the cut list equals `sum of all panel widths + sum of all gaps between panels`.
- All other part properties (material, profile, finish, etc.) are taken from the first panel's rail.
- Non-rail parts from each panel appear individually in the list, as usual.
- Only one row appears per rail category (one top rail, one bottom rail) for the entire group — not one per panel.

This ensures the cut list reflects the actual piece that goes through the machine, rather than individual per-panel lengths that would be incorrect.

::: tip Example
Two panels: 1200 mm and 900 mm wide, with a 10 mm gap between them.
Combined rail length = 1200 + 900 + 10 = **2110 mm**.
The BoM shows one top rail and one bottom rail, each 2110 mm long.
:::

## Machine File Impact (MOB2)

When generating a MOB2 machine file for a batch or selection that includes assemblies from a **locked** Multipanel Group:

- A **single `.mob2` file** is generated for the entire group, named after the group.
- The file is placed in the batch folder as `<phase>/<batch>/<group_name>.mob2`.
- Part positions within the combined file are offset correctly: parts from panel 2 are placed after panel 1, with the configured gap applied — so the machine sees the full combined run in the correct order.
- The revision field is left blank for group files (since a group has no single design revision).
- If only some assemblies of a locked group are included in the selection, the group is still treated as a whole — the file covers all panels in the group.

## Suggest Groups

Use the **Suggest** function on a batch to automatically find candidate groups. The suggestion engine scans the batch's production priority order with a sliding window and runs lightweight validation (skipping the framing and panel-layer checks) to surface likely valid combinations, sorted by start priority.

Suggestions are not saved automatically — review them and create the ones that make sense for your production run.

## Tracking Production Progress

Both the left-menu list (in the 3D viewer) and the **Multipanel Groups** management table show a row of small **station chips** for each group. Each chip represents one station of the batch's production line and shows the share of panels that have reached that station, in the form `ready/total`:

- An **outlined** chip means no panel has touched the station yet.
- A **filled warning** chip means some panels are working there or already past it.
- A **filled success** chip means every panel of the group has been marked ready at that station.
- When every station of every panel is ready, a single **`ready`** chip replaces the row.

Hover any chip to see the full breakdown — number of panels that are ready, currently working, and still waiting at that station.

## Clearing Proofs in Bulk

In the **Multipanel Groups** management table, ticking the checkbox of one or more rows reveals a **Proof Options** menu in the toolbar. The **Clear Proof** action wipes all production proofs (RCPs) for every panel of the selected groups in one operation — useful when a group needs to be reworked from the start. The same menu also offers **Set Ready** and **Merge Checklist**, mirroring the actions available on individual constructibles.

pages.title: IFC Parsing Setup
pages.body:
# IFC Parsing Setup (IFC PS)

::: info Why this exists
The IFC standard is open and versatile, and every BIM application exports it in
its own way. What one exporter calls `REFERENCE` another writes as a property
set value, and a stud can be recognised by its name in one file and by its
profile in the next. An IFC Parsing Setup is how you tell produuz.it to read
**your** files.
:::

A company can have several setups, and **each project uses one**. Open them in
**Company settings → IFC Parsing Setups**.

Every setting has an **(i)** button that opens the help panel on the right,
with the same explanation you find here plus a typical example. The panel
follows whatever you pressed last, so you can leave it open while you work.

::: tip Let Claude write it for you
Building a setup from scratch is the slowest part of onboarding, and it is what
the **Claude connector** is most useful for. Give Claude the property list of a
few elements from your BIM application, describe your panels in your own words,
and ask it for the setup. It writes a JSON file you upload with the **UPLOAD**
button, and you check it tab by tab before saving.

See: [The setup file (JSON)](/guide/management/ifcps/json/) ·
[Claude connector (MCP)](/guide/mcp/)
:::

## How a setup is organised

The editor has seven tabs, in this order:

| Tab | What you set there |
| --- | ------------------ |
| [Hierarchy and project](#hierarchy-and-project) | How the file is split into modules and panels, where the names, phases and batches come from, and which assemblies are produced at all |
| [Custom part branches](#custom-part-branches) | Your own kinds of part beyond the built-in ones |
| [Panel part categories](#panel-part-categories) | Which elements are rails, studs, plates, bricks, openings and areas |
| [Steel cage part categories](#steel-cage-part-categories) | The same, for the steel cage flow |
| [Part properties](#part-properties) | Where each value of a part is read from |
| [Custom part classes](#custom-part-classes) | Kinds of part you tell apart inside a category, and what they do to the panel measurements |
| [Operations and machines](#operations-and-machines) | Which elements are nail lines, cuts and drills, and what the machine files read |

The filter box at the top left of each tab searches the settings by name, and
also by the values inside their rules, so typing `STIJL` lands on every rule
that uses it.

## The two kinds of entry

Almost everything in a setup is one of two things.

### Rules

Used by categories, by the assembly filter and by the machine flags. Each rule
has three fields:

- **IFC Prop** — the property to look into.
- **Type of match** — *Match full word*, *Match prefix* or *Contains word*.
- **Value** — what to look for.

A part matches the setting when **any one** of its rules matches.

::: tip Example
Two rules on the *Top Rail Wood* category:

| IFC Prop  | Type of match | Value   |
| --------- | ------------- | ------- |
| REFERENCE | Match full word | TOPRAIL |
| REFERENCE | Match prefix    | TR      |

Parts with a `REFERENCE` of **TOPRAIL**, **TR**, **TR12** or **TR45** are top
rails. `TOPRAIL2`, `TOP_RAIL` and `12TR` are not.
:::

### Property names

Used by the properties. Here you only list the **IFC property names** that may
hold the value, in order of preference. The first one present on the element
wins.

::: tip Example
Two names on the *Zone (layer)* property, `WorkPlane` and `Layer`:

| Part | `WorkPlane` | `Layer`   | Detected zone |
| ---- | ----------- | --------- | ------------- |
| P1   | 1           | 2         | 1             |
| P2   | *(absent)*  | 3         | 3             |
| P3   | 1           | *(absent)* | 1            |
:::

::: warning Case does not matter
Property names and values are matched **case-insensitively**. `Reference`,
`REFERENCE` and `reference` are the same thing.
:::

### Reading from a specific property set

By default produuz.it looks for a property **anywhere in the element**: in any
of its property sets, and among the element's own attributes. That is what you
want almost always.

It becomes a problem when the same property name exists in two property sets
with different values — the exporter's `REFERENCE` and your own `REFERENCE`,
say. Then it is luck which one is read.

Every rule and every property name has a **Read from a specific property set**
checkbox for that case:

| Checkbox | Field | What is read |
| -------- | ----- | ------------ |
| unticked | — | The property wherever it appears. The normal case. |
| ticked | `Tekla_Common` | That property set only. Another set carrying a property of the same name is ignored. |
| ticked | *(left empty)* | The element's own attributes only: `name`, `ifc_tag`, `ifc_id`, `object_type`, `description`. |

Tick it when you have a reason to. An unticked entry behaves exactly as it
always has, and setups saved before this existed are untouched.

## Hierarchy and project

How the file is split, what the pieces are called, and which of them you
actually produce.

### Levels detection {#levels-detection}

Says how elements are grouped into modules, assemblies and subassemblies:
either by an **IFC class** (usually `IfcElementAssembly`) or by the value of a
**property**, for exporters that write no containers at all.

### Unit and project properties {#unit-and-project-properties}

*Levels detection* above says how a module and an assembly are recognised.
These say what is read from each one once it has been: what it is called, which
phase and batch it belongs to, and any extra values of yours that should travel
with it.

They are read off the **container** — the module or the assembly — and not off
its parts. Everything read off a part is in the
[Part properties](#part-properties) tab.

Leave one empty and produuz.it falls back to its own default, which for a name
is the container element's own name.

#### Module name {#module-name}

The properties holding the module design name, for example `Modulenummer`.
Instances of the same design share this value.

#### Module unit ID {#module-unit-id}

The properties holding the unique id of each module instance. Without it,
modules sharing a name are merged into one and you get a warning.

#### Assembly name {#assembly-name}

The properties holding the panel name. Left empty, the container's own name is
used.

#### Phase Name {#phase-name}

The property holding the phase a panel belongs to. Phases and batches are
created from these values when the file is split.

#### Batch Name {#batch-name}

The property holding the batch a panel belongs to.

#### Auto Parsed Client Meta {#auto-parsed-client-meta}

Properties copied onto the design as client data when the file is analysed.
Useful for anything of yours that has no field of its own.

### Assembly filter

A project file usually holds more than you produce: foundations, in-situ
concrete, the building next door. Two lists decide what the splitter takes out
of it.

#### Split only these assemblies {#split-only-these-assemblies}

Leave it empty and **every** assembly is split. With rules in it, only the
assemblies matching one of them are split out.

#### Never split these assemblies {#never-split-these-assemblies}

Assemblies matching one of these are never split out, **even when the first
list keeps them**. The drop list always wins, which is how you keep a whole
prefix and still leave a few names out of it.

An assembly that is not split leaves nothing behind: no IFC file, no design,
and nothing in the phase and batch counts.

::: details Example
*Split only these assemblies:* `ASSEMBLY_PREFIX` starts with `WA`

*Never split these assemblies:* `name` contains `_TEST`

You get every wall except the ones whose name carries `_TEST`. Roofs, floors
and everything else in the file are left alone.
:::

## Custom part branches {#custom-part-branches}

Branches are kinds of part beyond the built-in timber and plate: windows,
connectors, airtightness, electrical, plumbing.

Each branch has a name, its own rules, the geometry it **resembles** —
wood-like, plate-like or generic, so drawings, counts and cutting lists know
how to treat it — and two switches.

### Logistics enabled {#branch-logistics}

The parts of this branch reach the **parts list** and go through logistics.

### Counts in the panel measurements {#branch-in-metrics}

The parts of this branch take part in the panel **width, height, thickness and
surface**.

This exists because a branch is recognised *before* a part falls back to
timber, plate or steel from its category. A part your setup recognises
perfectly well as a window frame or a cladding profile can therefore have no
category at all, and a part with no category is outside every measurement —
which is why a panel can read thinner or smaller than it is, with no warning.

Leave it **off** for brackets, connectors and anything that sticks out past
the frame: counting those makes the panel read wider and taller than it is.
Turn it **on** for cladding, window frames and layers that are really part of
the panel.

::: info The measurements are not only a report figure
The **rack loads** are drawn from them. The width decides how many panels fit
in a rack row and the thickness how deep the stack builds, so a panel measured
short is a rack plan that does not fit on the floor.
See: [Delivery & Racks](/guide/logistics/delivery/)
:::

::: info It only decides whether the part takes part at all
Which measurements it is then left out of is a **custom part class** job. A
window frame that should set the thickness but add no surface gets the switch
here *and* a class with *Ignore in surface*. The branch says whether the part
participates; the class says what it is out of.
See: [Custom part classes](#custom-part-classes)
:::

::: info Both switches are off by default
Turning this on changes the measurements of every panel holding parts of that
branch, from its next analysis. Nothing moves until you tick it.
:::

## Panel part categories

The elements that make up a prefabricated panel. Every rule here matches the
**raw IFC properties** of the element — its Name, Reference, Material and the
rest, exactly as the modeller exported them.

### Frame

#### Top Rail Wood {#top-rail-wood}

The horizontal wood at the top of the frame. The studs are nailed into it from
above and the panel height is measured from its outer face.

#### Bottom Rail Wood {#bottom-rail-wood}

The horizontal wood at the bottom of the frame. The panel's zero height is its
outer face.

#### Extra Top Wood {#extra-top-wood}

Woods over the top rail, usually fitted after the studs are nailed.

#### Extra Bottom Wood {#extra-bottom-wood}

Woods below the bottom rail, usually fitted after the studs are nailed.

#### Wood profile {#wood-profile}

Any wood of the frame that is not a rail, a batten or an extra piece: the
studs, noggins and diagonals. This is the category the framing nail matrix
applies to.

#### Extra Frame Wood profile {#extra-frame-wood-profile}

Additional frame woods that are not part of the standard framing.

#### Wood Batten {#wood-batten}

Battens fixed on the panel.

### Plates

#### Plate {#plate}

A sheet fixed on a face of the frame: OSB, plasterboard, fibreboard. Its layer
decides the zone it is machined in.

#### Core Plate {#core-plate}

A plate inside the frame rather than on a face, such as a shear panel.

### Other parts

#### Bricks / Stones {#bricks-stones}

Single bricks or stones.

#### Opening {#opening}

Placeholders for doors and windows. They are not produced; they tell the
machines where the frame has a hole and give the reports their opening list.

### Areas and flags

Elements that are not produced but change how a panel is handled.

#### Lockout Area {#lockout-area}

Areas the machine must not work on.

#### Isolated Area {#isolated-area}

Areas that carry insulation.

#### Skip Framing Wood {#skip-framing-wood}

Parts that would fall into the frame by geometry but must not be counted as
framing wood.

::: info Hiding and ignoring a part are on the classes now
*Hidden Material* and *Ignored Part* used to be categories here. They never said
what a part **is**, they said how to treat it, so they are
[class behaviours](#class-behaviours) — *Ignore this part completely* and *Hide
in the 3D viewer*. Setups that had the old categories were moved across and
behave exactly as they did.

*Not Isolated Area* is gone too. Nothing ever read it.
:::

## Steel cage part categories

A secondary flow. Leave it empty if you do not produce steel cages.

#### Top Steel Profile {#top-steel-profile}

#### Bottom Steel Profile {#bottom-steel-profile}

#### Steel Profile {#steel-profile}

#### Steel Plate {#steel-plate}

#### Welding Seam {#welding-seam}

#### Compute holes {#compute-holes}

Whether the holes of the profile are computed for the machine file.

#### Assembly ID Level1 {#assembly-id-level1}

#### Assembly ID Level2 {#assembly-id-level2}

The two levels of assembly id of a steel cage.

## Part properties {#part-properties}

Where produuz.it reads each value of a part from. Each entry is a list of IFC
property names, tried in order.

### Identity

#### Part Name {#part-name}

The name produuz.it uses for the part, shown in the parts list, the reports and
the machine file templates.

Leave it empty and the part keeps the name the IFC element itself carries. Fill
it in when the useful name lives in a property set instead, for example
`ELEMENT_NAME` or `Beschrijving`.

- **The IFC name is always kept.** It stays visible in the part drawer, in the
  *Unknown parts* dialog of the viewer, and as its own optional column in the
  parts list.
- **It does not change how parts are classified.** The category and branch
  rules always match against the raw IFC properties. To match on the property
  you mapped here, add a rule on that property's own key.

#### Reference {#reference}

An id expected to be the same across parts of the same shape. Usually
`reference` in Tekla Structures, and available in other exporters too.

#### Material Name {#material-name}

The material of the part.

#### Profile Name {#profile-name}

The name of the shaped section, for profiles that are not rectangular.

#### Profile Joined {#profile-joined}

Whether the profile is extended or joined to another one.

### Zone (layer) {#zone-layer}

The panel layer a part belongs to. `0` is the frame, and the layers on each
face are numbered outwards from it: `1`, `2` on one side and `-1`, `-2` on the
other.

Most IFC files write that layer with a letter instead of a sign, usually `F`
for the front face and `B` for the back one. produuz.it reads the letter: a
value holding a **`B`** becomes a negative zone, and anything else stays
positive.

| IFC value | Detected zone |
| --------- | ------------- |
| `F1`      | 1             |
| `F2`      | 2             |
| `B1`      | -1            |
| `B2`      | -2            |
| `Back2`   | -2            |
| `1`       | 1             |
| `-1`      | -1            |

Letters and other characters are stripped, so only the `B` changes the result.
A value that already carries a minus sign is used as it is.

::: warning
The `B` rule applies to every **numeric** property, not only the zone. Keep a
`B` out of the values you map to *Nail/Screw CTC*, *Mill/Saw depth*, *Isolation
order number* and *Tool ID*, because it would turn them negative.
:::

#### Positive side zones {#positive-side-zones}

#### Negative side zones {#negative-side-zones}

**BTLx only.** BTLx layer numbers come as plain numbers with no sign, so these
two rule lists declare which layers belong to each face of the panel.

### Details

#### Finish {#finish}

The finish of the part.

#### Comment {#comment}

A free comment shown with the part.

#### Weight (kg) {#weight-kg}

The weight of the part in kg. Some exporters write it in the element property
sets (`Weight`, `GEWICHT`), others export only the volume.

#### Volume (m3) {#volume-m3}

The volume of the part in m³. Exported by nearly every application, and what a
weight can be derived from when the exporter writes none.

#### Isolation order number {#isolation-order-number}

The order in which insulation areas are filled.

## Custom part classes {#custom-part-classes}

A **category** says what a part is: a stud, a rail, a plate. A **class** says
how your factory treats it. They are two different questions, and a part
answers both at once.

Classes are entirely your own. Nothing is built in and nothing is detected
automatically: a part is an I-beam only because a rule you wrote says so.

Give each class a name and add the rules that recognise it, with the same kind
of rule as the categories. A part gets the **first class in the list whose
rules match**, so put the more specific classes first. A part that matches no
class simply has none, and that is normal.

A class does two things.

**Its name** is what other settings look up when they behave differently per
kind of part — the framing nail matrix of the machine setups first of all.
See: [Mobi One](/guide/machine_files/machines/mobi_one/)

**Its behaviours** say what the class does to the panel measurements. That is
the *Behaviours* button on each class.

### Behaviours {#class-behaviours}

Every panel carries four measurements: its width, its height, its thickness and
its surface. By default every part counts in all four. A behaviour takes the
parts of one class out of one of them — or out of produuz.it altogether.

**Whole part**

| Behaviour | What it does |
| --------- | ------------ |
| Ignore this part completely | The part never reaches the parts list, the reports or the machine files. Use it for helper geometry, annotations and anything the modeller exported by accident. |
| Hide in the 3D viewer | The part is still measured and still produced, it is only not drawn. Use it for insulation, foils and fillers that would cover the frame. |

**Measurements**

| Behaviour | What it leaves the part out of |
| --------- | ------------------------------ |
| Ignore in surface | The net area, the gross area and the opening areas of the panel |
| Ignore in width (X) | The width of the panel |
| Ignore in height (Y) | The height of the panel |
| Ignore in thickness (Z) | The thickness of the panel |

They are all **off by default, and off means the part counts** — which is what
every part did before behaviours existed. Turning none on changes nothing.

::: info The measurements are not only a report figure
The **rack loads** are drawn from them. The width decides how many panels fit
in a rack row and the thickness how deep the stack builds, so a panel measured
short is a rack plan that does not fit on the floor.
See: [Delivery & Racks](/guide/logistics/delivery/)
:::

The four are separate because the measurements are separate, and that is what
makes the useful cases possible.

::: info Placeholder layers
The case behaviours were built for. Some modellers add a layer to a panel that
is not produced but occupies the space a real one will take — an insulation
layer, a finish, a service cavity.

That layer has to count for the **thickness**, because the panel really is that
thick. It must not count for the **surface**, because nothing was produced.

Give it a class, turn on *Ignore in surface*, *Ignore in width* and *Ignore in
height*, and leave *Ignore in thickness* **off**. The panel keeps its real
thickness and its surface stops counting a layer nobody built.
:::

::: info A part that sticks out
A bracket or an anchor that reaches past the edge of the panel makes it read
wider than it is. Give it a class and turn on *Ignore in width*, and only that
one. It still counts everywhere else.
:::

The class row shows what it ignores without opening anything, so a setup is
readable at a glance.

::: info When the numbers change
Panel measurements are worked out during the **analysis** of a design, not when
you look at them. Saving the setup relaunches the analysis of the projects that
use it, and the new numbers appear when it finishes.

If your company has *Launch analysis automatically* turned off in the company
settings, nothing is relaunched and the old numbers stay until you launch the
analysis yourself.
:::

## Operations and machines

Nail lines, saw cuts, drills and glue are modelled as elements too. These rules
tell them apart from parts, and the properties below feed the machine files
directly.

::: info They are never measured
An operation says what a machine does, not what the panel is made of, so
nothing here counts towards the width, height, thickness or surface of a panel.
A saw mark that hangs below the bottom rail does not make the panel taller.
:::

### Operation lines

#### Frame Nail Lines {#frame-nail-lines}

A group of frame nails represented as a line. The line goes through the heads
of the nails.

#### Frame Nail Singles {#frame-nail-singles}

A single frame nail represented as a line. The line goes through the body of
the nail.

#### Plate Nail Lines {#plate-nail-lines}

The same as frame nail lines, for nails into the plates.

#### Plate Screw {#plate-screw}

Lines representing screws, read like the nail lines.

#### Glue lines {#glue-lines}

Glue lines, used for bricks.

#### Glue areas {#glue-areas}

Areas to be covered with glue.

### Cutting and milling

#### Frame Saw {#frame-saw}

Saw cuts on the frame.

#### Frame Drill {#frame-drill}

Drills on the frame.

#### Milling {#milling}

Milling lines.

#### Sawing {#sawing}

Sawing lines on the plates.

#### Drilling {#drilling}

Drilling operations.

### Machine parameters

#### Nail/Screw CTC {#nailscrew-ctc}

The centre-to-centre distance in nail and screw lines.

#### Mill/Saw depth {#millsaw-depth}

The depth of a milling or sawing line.

#### Tool ID for mob2 nailing {#tool-id-for-mob2-nailing}

The tool the MOB2 machine must use for the nailing.

#### Frame Saw Size {#frame-saw-size}

The side of the frame the saw works on.

#### Brick Type {#brick-type}

The type of the brick.

### Machine flags

Each of these has an IFC property and, beside it, a BTLx rule list that does
the same job for BTLx files.

#### Bricks: Machine Flag {#bricks-machine-flag}

#### Bricks: Machine Flag (BTLx) {#bricks-machine-flag-btlx}

A brick that is machine built rather than laid by hand.

#### Isolation: Machine Flag {#isolation-machine-flag}

#### Isolation: Machine Flag (BTLx) {#isolation-machine-flag-btlx}

Insulation applied by the machine.

#### Battens: Machine Flag {#battens-machine-flag}

#### Battens: Machine Flag (BTLx) {#battens-machine-flag-btlx}

Battens fitted by the machine.

#### Milling: V-Mill {#milling-v-mill}

#### Milling: V-Mill (BTLx) {#milling-v-mill-btlx}

A milling line that must be done as a V-mill.

::: info Skip Framing Wood is on the other tab
It follows the same pattern — one IFC property and one BTLx rule list beside it
— but it sits with the areas and flags, on
[Panel part categories](#skip-framing-wood).
:::

## BTLx files

BTLx files are read with the same setup, with two differences:

- **No property sets.** BTLx parts carry plain attributes, so the *Read from a
  specific property set* checkbox is not offered on the BTLx rules, and a rule
  that names a property set never matches a BTLx part.
- **Zones need declaring.** BTLx layer numbers have no sign, so the face of the
  panel comes from the [Positive side zones](#positive-side-zones) and
  [Negative side zones](#negative-side-zones) rules instead of from a letter.

The settings that are BTLx-only are marked with a **BTLx** chip in the editor.

## Saving

The setup is validated before it is saved. If something is missing — a rule
with an empty value, typically — you get a message and the editor opens the tab
holding the offending field and scrolls to it.

::: warning Saving relaunches the analysis
Saving a setup used by projects relaunches their analysis, so the parts are
re-read with the new rules. The editor warns you before it does.
:::

## Moving a setup around

The **↓** button on a setup row downloads it as a JSON file, and **UPLOAD** in
the toolbar reads one back in. That is how you copy a setup between companies,
keep a version outside the platform, or have Claude write one for you.

Uploading saves nothing on its own: the file opens in this same editor, and it
exists when you press Save.

See: [The setup file (JSON)](/guide/management/ifcps/json/)

pages.title: The setup file (JSON)
pages.body:
# The setup file (JSON)

A parsing setup can be **downloaded as a JSON file and uploaded back**. The file
holds every rule of the setup, so it is how you move a setup between companies,
keep a copy outside the platform, or write a setup somewhere else and bring it
in finished.

This page is the reference for that file: every field, every key, and what a
value has to look like for the platform to read it.

::: tip You do not have to write it by hand
Claude can write the whole file for you from a sample IFC and a description of
your panels. See [Let Claude write it](#let-claude-write-it) at the end of this
page.
:::

[[toc]]

## Download and upload

Both live in **Company settings → IFC Parsing Setups**.

| Action | Where | What it does |
| ------ | ----- | ------------ |
| Download | The **↓** button on a setup row | Saves `ifcps_<name>.json`. The uuid and the company are stripped, so the file describes rules and nothing else. |
| Upload | **UPLOAD** in the toolbar | Reads the file and **opens the editor filled in with it**. |

Uploading saves nothing on its own. The file lands in the normal editor, you
check it tab by tab, and it exists only when you press **Save**.

::: warning A uuid in the file overwrites that setup
A downloaded file carries no `uuid`, so uploading it always creates a **new**
setup. If you add a `uuid` by hand, saving overwrites the setup with that uuid
and re-analyses every project using it. Leave it out.
:::

## The two building blocks

Almost every value in the file is one of two things.

### A rule

Used by the categories, the assembly filter, the machine flags, the branches and
the classes. Three keys:

```json
{ "prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "TR" }
```

| Key | Value |
| --- | ----- |
| `prop_key` | The property to look into. Any property name the file carries, or one of the five element attributes below. Case does not matter. |
| `match` | `"all"`, `"prefix"` or `"contains"`. |
| `value` | What to look for. Case does not matter. |

| `match` | Matches when the property value |
| ------- | ------------------------------- |
| `all` | is exactly this value |
| `prefix` | starts with this value |
| `contains` | holds this value anywhere |

A part matches a setting when **any one** of its rules matches. A rule whose
`prop_key` the element does not carry never matches, and neither does one whose
`match` is missing or misspelled.

::: danger Never leave `value` empty
An empty `value` with `match` set to `prefix` or `contains` matches **every**
element that carries the property, because every string starts with nothing and
holds nothing. A whole category would swallow the panel.

The editor refuses to save a rule with an empty value, so an uploaded file is
caught before it does any harm — but it is caught as a red field on some tab you
have to go and find. Do not write one.
:::

The five element attributes are always available as `prop_key`, whatever the
file's property sets are called:

`name` · `ifc_tag` · `ifc_id` · `object_type` · `description`

Everything else has to be a property the exporter actually wrote: `reference`,
`zone`, `profile` and the rest are only useful if your IFC carries a property
with that name.

### A property name list

Used by everything under `props`, `steel_props` and `project_props`. Here you do
not match, you say **where to read a value from**: a list of property names,
tried in order, first one present on the element wins.

```json
"weight": ["WEIGHT", "GEWICHT"]
```

### Reading from one property set only

Both blocks take an optional `pset`, for the case where two property sets carry
the same property name with different values.

```json
{ "prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "TR", "pset": "Tekla_Common" }
{ "key": "ZONE", "pset": "Pset_WallCommon" }
```

| `pset` | What is read |
| ------ | ------------ |
| absent | The property wherever it appears. The normal case. |
| `"Tekla_Common"` | That property set only. |
| `""` | The element's own attributes only. |

A property name list takes the plain string form `"ZONE"` or the scoped form
`{"key": "ZONE", "pset": "..."}`, and you can mix both in the same list.

::: info BTLx files have no property sets
The same setup reads BTLx files, where `prop_key` is the name of an attribute on
the BTLx part (`Designation`, `Material`, `Group`). A scoped entry never matches
a BTLx part.
:::

## Top-level fields

```json
{
  "name": "Tekla Wall Panels",
  "is_default": false,
  "setup": {},
  "props": {},
  "steel_setup": {},
  "steel_props": {},
  "project_setup": {},
  "project_props": {},
  "level_setup": {},
  "custom_branches": [],
  "part_classes": []
}
```

| Field | Type | Holds |
| ----- | ---- | ----- |
| `name` | string, **max 22 characters** | The setup name. Required. |
| `is_default` | boolean | Whether new projects start from this setup. Only one setup per company can be the default. |
| `setup` | object | Panel part categories, operations and machine flags. Rule lists. |
| `props` | object | Part properties. Property name lists. |
| `steel_setup` | object | Steel cage categories. Rule lists. |
| `steel_props` | object | Steel cage properties. Property name lists. |
| `project_setup` | object | The assembly filter. Rule lists. |
| `project_props` | object | What is read off a module or an assembly. Property name lists. |
| `level_setup` | object | How the file is split into levels, plus the BTLx zone rules. |
| `custom_branches` | array | Your own kinds of part. |
| `part_classes` | array | Your own classes and their behaviours. |

Every one of them may be left out, and an empty object or list is valid. A
category with no rules simply recognises nothing.

::: details Fields you can ignore
`wood_setup`, `wood_props`, `concrete_setup`, `concrete_props`, `custom_setup`,
`custom_props` and `level_props` exist in the file for compatibility. The editor
writes to none of them. Leave them out.

`read_only` and `company_lock` are locks, not rules. Leave them out too.
:::

## `setup` — categories, operations and flags

Every key holds a **list of rules**.

::: danger A mistyped key here is not ignored
The rules under it still run, and a part matching one is filed under a category
nothing recognises: it drops out of the parts list, the measurements, the reports
and the machine files without a word. It can also **outrank a correct rule** and
take a part away from the category it belonged in.

Check every key against the tables below. This is the single most common way a
hand-written setup goes wrong.
:::

### Frame

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `top_rail` | The horizontal wood at the top of the frame |
| `bottom_rail` | The horizontal wood at the bottom |
| `extra_top_rail` | Woods over the top rail |
| `extra_bottom_rail` | Woods below the bottom rail |
| `wood` | Any other frame wood: studs, noggins, diagonals |
| `extra_wood` | Frame woods outside the standard framing |
| `batten` | Battens fixed on the panel |

### Plates

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `plate` | A sheet on a face of the frame |
| `core_plate` | A plate inside the frame |

### Other parts

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `brick` | Single bricks or stones |
| `opening` | Door and window placeholders, not produced |

### Areas and flags

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `lockout_area` | Areas the machine must not work on |
| `isolated_area` | Areas that carry insulation |
| `skip_framing_wood` | BTLx parts that must not be counted as framing wood |

### Operation lines

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `frame_nail` | Frame nail lines |
| `frame_nail_single` | Single frame nails |
| `plate_nail` | Plate nail lines |
| `plate_screw` | Plate screws |
| `glue` | Glue lines |
| `glue_area` | Glue areas |

### Cutting and milling

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `frame_saw` | Saw cuts on the frame |
| `frame_drill` | Drills on the frame |
| `milling` | Milling lines |
| `sawing` | Sawing lines on the plates |
| `drilling` | Drilling operations |

### Machine flags (BTLx)

Each one mirrors a property of the same job under `props`, for files that carry
attributes instead of properties.

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `brick_machine_flag` | Bricks built by the machine |
| `isolation_machine_flag` | Insulation applied by the machine |
| `battens_machine_flag` | Battens fitted by the machine |
| `v_mill` | Milling lines done as a V-mill |

::: info Two keys that used to live here
`ignore_me` and `hidden_material` were categories and are now **class
behaviours** — `skip_everything` and `hide_in_viewer` on a
[part class](#part-classes). A setup written today should use the classes; old
files keep working. `not_isolated_area` was never read by anything.
:::

## `props` — part properties

Every key holds a **list of property names**. Unlike `setup`, a key that is not
in this table is read by nothing — silently, so the property simply comes out
empty and nothing says why.

| Key | What it reads |
| --- | ------------- |
| `name` | The part name. Left out, the element's own Name is used. |
| `fab_ref` | The reference, expected to be the same for parts of the same shape |
| `material` | The material name |
| `shaped_section_name` | The profile name, for sections that are not rectangular |
| `profile_joined` | Whether the profile is extended or joined |
| `zone` | The panel layer the part belongs to |
| `finish` | The finish |
| `comment` | A free comment |
| `weight` | The weight in kg |
| `volume` | The volume in m³ |
| `isolation_order` | The order insulation areas are filled in |
| `nail_ctc` | Centre-to-centre distance in nail and screw lines |
| `mill_depth` | Depth of a milling or sawing line |
| `nail_tool_id` | The tool the MOB2 machine nails with |
| `frame_saw_side` | The side of the frame the saw works on |
| `brick_type` | The type of brick |
| `is_machine_brick` | Bricks built by the machine |
| `is_machine_isolation` | Insulation applied by the machine |
| `is_machine_battens` | Battens fitted by the machine |
| `is_vmill` | Milling lines done as a V-mill |
| `skip_framing_wood` | Parts not to be counted as framing wood |

::: warning The zone reads a letter as a sign
A zone value holding a **`B`** becomes a negative zone; anything else stays
positive, and letters are stripped. So `F1` is `1` and `B2` is `-2`.

That rule applies to **every numeric property**, so keep a `B` out of the values
you map to `nail_ctc`, `mill_depth`, `isolation_order` and `nail_tool_id`.
:::

## `steel_setup` and `steel_props`

Only for the steel cage flow. Leave both out if you do not produce steel cages.

| `steel_setup` key | What it is |
| ----------------- | ---------- |
| `top_steel_rail` | Top steel profile |
| `bottom_steel_rail` | Bottom steel profile |
| `steel_profile` | Any other steel profile |
| `steel_plate` | Steel plate |
| `steel_welding_seam` | Welding seam |

| `steel_props` key | What it reads |
| ----------------- | ------------- |
| `steel_compute_holes` | Whether the holes of the profile are computed |
| `assembly_id` | Assembly id, level 1 |
| `assembly_id2` | Assembly id, level 2 |

## `project_props` — read off a module or an assembly

Property name lists, read off the **container**, not off its parts.

| Key | What it reads |
| --- | ------------- |
| `module_design_name` | The module design name. Instances of the same design share it. |
| `custom_module_id` | The unique id of each module instance |
| `assembly_design_name` | The panel name. Left out, the container's own name is used. |
| `phase_name` | The phase a panel belongs to |
| `batch_name` | The batch a panel belongs to |
| `client_meta` | Properties copied onto the design as client data |

## `project_setup` — the assembly filter

Two rule lists deciding which assemblies are split out of the project file.

```json
"project_setup": {
  "assembly_filter":     [{"prop_key": "ASSEMBLY_PREFIX", "match": "prefix", "value": "WA"}],
  "assembly_filter_out": [{"prop_key": "name", "match": "contains", "value": "_TEST"}]
}
```

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | ------- |
| `assembly_filter` | Empty or absent, every assembly is split. With rules, **only** matching assemblies are split. |
| `assembly_filter_out` | Matching assemblies are never split, even when the first list keeps them. |

The drop list always wins. An assembly that is not split produces nothing: no
IFC file, no design, no row in the phase and batch counts.

## `level_setup` — how the file is split

Three levels, each an object rather than a list of rules.

```json
"level_setup": {
  "module":      { "detection": "ifc_class", "match": "IfcElementAssembly" },
  "assembly":    { "detection": "ifc_class", "match": "IfcElementAssembly" },
  "subassembly": { "detection": "part_prop", "match": "SUBASSEMBLY" }
}
```

| `detection` | `match` is |
| ----------- | ---------- |
| `ifc_class` | An IFC class name: `IfcElementAssembly`, `IfcWall`, `IfcSlab`, `IfcPresentationLayerAssignment` |
| `part_prop` | A property name read off the parts |
| `ass_prop` | A property name read off the assembly |

The same object also holds two more keys, each a plain **list of rules**, because
BTLx layer numbers carry no sign and the face of the panel has to be declared.

| Key | What it is |
| --- | ---------- |
| `positive_zone` | BTLx layers on the reference face of the panel |
| `negative_zone` | BTLx layers on the opposite face |

```json
"positive_zone": [{"prop_key": "Layer", "match": "all", "value": "1"}],
"negative_zone": [{"prop_key": "Layer", "match": "all", "value": "2"}]
```

They do nothing for IFC files, where the zone sign comes from the `zone`
property instead.

## `custom_branches`

Kinds of part beyond the built-in timber and plate: windows, connectors,
airtightness, electrical, plumbing.

```json
"custom_branches": [
  {
    "name": "windows",
    "alike": "generic",
    "logistics": true,
    "metrics": true,
    "entries": [{"prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "WIN"}]
  }
]
```

| Key | Value |
| --- | ----- |
| `name` | The branch name. Lowercased everywhere it is used. |
| `alike` | `"generic"`, `"plate"` or `"wood"` — the geometry it resembles, so drawings and cutting lists know how to treat it. |
| `logistics` | `true` puts its parts in the parts list and through logistics. Default `false`. |
| `metrics` | `true` counts its parts in the panel width, height, thickness and surface. Default `false`. |
| `entries` | The rules that recognise it. |

::: warning `metrics` is off by default and that has consequences
A branch is recognised **before** a part falls back to timber or plate from its
category, so a part your setup knows perfectly well can end up with no category
— and a part with no category is outside every panel measurement.

Turn `metrics` on for cladding and window frames. Leave it off for brackets and
anything that sticks out past the frame.
:::

## `part_classes`

A category says what a part is. A class says how your factory treats it. A part
gets the **first class in the list whose rules match**, so put the more specific
classes first.

```json
"part_classes": [
  {
    "name": "Placeholder",
    "entries": [{"prop_key": "name", "match": "prefix", "value": "PLH"}],
    "behaviours": {"skip_area": true, "skip_x": true, "skip_y": true}
  }
]
```

| Key | Value |
| --- | ----- |
| `name` | The class name. Settings that behave differently per kind of part, the framing nail matrix first, look it up by this. |
| `entries` | The rules that recognise it. |
| `behaviours` | Optional. Absent means the part behaves normally. |

| Behaviour | What it does |
| --------- | ------------ |
| `skip_area` | The part is left out of the net, gross and opening areas |
| `skip_x` | Left out of the panel width |
| `skip_y` | Left out of the panel height |
| `skip_z` | Left out of the panel thickness |
| `skip_everything` | The part is ignored completely: no parts list, no reports, no machine files |
| `hide_in_viewer` | Still measured and still produced, only not drawn in the 3D viewer |

All of them are `false` when absent, and `false` means the part counts. Only the
keys you turn on need to be in the file.

::: info The placeholder case
A layer that is not produced but takes up the space a real one will: it has to
count for the **thickness**, because the panel really is that thick, and not for
the **surface**, because nothing was produced. Turn on `skip_area`, `skip_x` and
`skip_y`, and leave `skip_z` off. That is the example above.
:::

## A complete example

A small but working setup. Every field it leaves out is simply not used.

```json
{
  "name": "Tekla Wall Panels",
  "level_setup": {
    "module":   { "detection": "ifc_class", "match": "IfcElementAssembly" },
    "assembly": { "detection": "ifc_class", "match": "IfcElementAssembly" }
  },
  "project_props": {
    "assembly_design_name": ["ASSEMBLY_NAME"],
    "phase_name": ["PHASE"],
    "batch_name": ["BATCH"]
  },
  "project_setup": {
    "assembly_filter_out": [
      { "prop_key": "name", "match": "contains", "value": "_TEST" }
    ]
  },
  "setup": {
    "top_rail": [
      { "prop_key": "reference", "match": "all", "value": "TOPRAIL" },
      { "prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "TR" }
    ],
    "bottom_rail": [
      { "prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "BR" }
    ],
    "wood": [
      { "prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "W" }
    ],
    "plate": [
      { "prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "P" }
    ],
    "opening": [
      { "prop_key": "name", "match": "contains", "value": "OPENING" }
    ],
    "frame_nail": [
      { "prop_key": "name", "match": "prefix", "value": "FNL" }
    ]
  },
  "props": {
    "fab_ref": ["REFERENCE"],
    "zone": ["ZONE", "LAYER"],
    "material": ["MATERIAL"],
    "weight": ["WEIGHT", "GEWICHT"],
    "volume": ["VOLUME", "NETVOLUME"],
    "nail_ctc": ["NAIL_CTC", "SCREW_CTC"]
  },
  "custom_branches": [
    {
      "name": "windows",
      "alike": "generic",
      "logistics": true,
      "metrics": true,
      "entries": [
        { "prop_key": "reference", "match": "prefix", "value": "WIN" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "part_classes": [
    {
      "name": "Placeholder",
      "entries": [
        { "prop_key": "name", "match": "prefix", "value": "PLH" }
      ],
      "behaviours": { "skip_area": true, "skip_x": true, "skip_y": true }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Before you upload

- `name` is present and **22 characters or fewer**.
- There is no `uuid`.
- Every key is one from the tables above. A mistyped key under `props` is read by
  nothing; a mistyped key under `setup` is worse, because its rules still run.
- Every rule has all three of `prop_key`, `match` and `value`, and `match` is one
  of `all`, `prefix`, `contains`. A misspelled `match` never matches anything.
- No rule has an empty `value`. The editor refuses to save one, and with
  `prefix` or `contains` it would have matched everything.
- Every `prop_key` and every property name is a property your IFC really carries.
  This is the one thing the file cannot tell you: check it against a sample file.

After uploading, walk the tabs before saving. The editor is the same one you
would have filled in by hand, and it validates the same way.

## Let Claude write it

produuz.it has a **Claude connector**, and writing a parsing setup is what it is
most useful for. Claude can read this documentation, so it knows every key on
this page and what each one is for.

Add the connector — see [Claude connector (MCP)](/guide/mcp/) — and then:

1. **Give it your properties.** Export the property list of a few elements from
   your BIM application — one stud, one rail, one plate, one panel — and paste it
   in. That list is what nearly every rule is written from.
2. **Describe your panels** in your own words: what marks a top rail, what marks
   a plate, which elements are not produced, where the phase and the batch come
   from.
3. **Ask for the file.** For example:

   > *Write me an IFC parsing setup JSON for produuz.it. Here are the properties
   > of four elements from our Tekla export. Top rails have REFERENCE starting
   > with TR, studs W, plates P. The phase is in the PHASE property of the
   > assembly. We do not produce steel cages.*

4. **Upload it** with the UPLOAD button and check every tab before saving.

Claude can also read a setup you already have. Download it, paste it in, and ask
why a part is landing in the wrong category or which rules are never used.

### Or let it create the setup directly

If you are a company administrator, Claude can skip the file and put the setup
straight into **Company settings → IFC Parsing Setups**. It asks for a separate
permission the first time, and you can say no and keep working with files.

What it creates is inert: no project uses it, nothing is re-analysed, and it cannot
touch a setup that already exists or make one the default. You still open it, walk
the tabs and assign it yourself. The checks on this page are not skipped either —
they are applied by the tool, so a key that is not in the tables above is refused
rather than stored.

See: [Creating a parsing setup](/guide/mcp/#creating-a-parsing-setup)

::: warning Always check what comes back
Claude cannot see your IFC file, only what you tell it about it. It writes the
rules; you check them against a real file. Nothing is saved until you press
**Save** in the editor, and the first real test is Step 9 of the
[setup tutorial](/tutorials/ifcps/): split a sample file and look for parts
landing in **unknown**.
:::

# Company Backup

The backup feature lets company admins generate a full export of their company data for safekeeping.

## Generating a Backup

1. Go to **Company Settings**.
2. Click **Generate Backup**.
3. The system will package all company data including projects, designs, constructibles, and configuration.

::: info
Backups are generated in the background. You'll be notified when the backup is ready for download.
:::

## What's Included

A company backup contains:

- All projects and their configurations
- Design data and constructible records
- Production line and station setups
- Report history
- Company settings and user configurations

pages.body:
# Production Planning

The Production Planning view lets you schedule constructibles (assemblies and modules) on a calendar, manage production priorities, and visualize workload across your production lines.

<!-- TODO: screenshot of the production planning calendar with constructibles scheduled -->

[[toc]]

## Calendar View

The calendar displays 1 to 4 months at a time, with each day showing the constructibles scheduled for production on that date. Items are ordered by priority within each day.

### Visual Indicators

- **Green** — Selected constructible.
- **Orange** — Modified (unsaved changes).
- **Red** — Overdue (past scheduled date, not yet produced).
- **Grey** — Past dates.
- **Blue** — Normal scheduled item.

## Scheduling Constructibles

### Drag and Drop

Drag a constructible from one date to another to reschedule it. You can also drag items from the **Unscheduled Constructibles** panel into the calendar.

### Priority

Within a single day, constructibles are produced in priority order (1 = first). Use the up/down arrows to reorder items within a date.

### Multi-Select

- **Ctrl+Click** — Select multiple individual items.
- **Shift+Click** — Select a range of items.

This allows you to move or modify several constructibles at once.

## Filters

- **Production line** — Show only constructibles assigned to a specific line.
- **Projects** — Filter by one or more projects.

## Settings

Click the settings icon to configure the calendar display:

| Setting | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| **Displayed months** | Show 1 to 4 months at a time. |
| **Calendar height** | Adjust the row height. |
| **Shown weekdays** | Choose which days of the week to display. |
| **Visible fields** | Select which data to show on each card (design name, UUID, client order, project, super-project, status). |
| **Workload display** | Toggle workload heatmap on calendar dates. |
| **Show ready items** | Show or hide already-completed constructibles. |

## Workload

When enabled, each calendar date shows a workload indicator based on the total expected production time for that day compared to the production line's capacity.

The workload is calculated from:
- Design area (m²) of each scheduled constructible
- Expected work time per m² at each station
- Production line's configured daily capacity (minutes per day)

::: tip
You can override the daily work capacity in the planning settings to model different scenarios (e.g., overtime, reduced shifts).
:::

## Saving Changes

After making scheduling changes, click **Save** to persist the updated dates and priorities. Unsaved changes are highlighted in orange.

pages.title: Quantities
pages.body:
# Quantities / BoM Matrix

The Quantities view lets you plan how many of each design to produce across project phases and batches. It uses a matrix layout where you define quantities before generating the actual constructibles.

<!-- TODO: screenshot of the quantities matrix with phases and design rows -->

[[toc]]

## Matrix Layout

The matrix is organized as:

- **Rows** — Design names (assemblies and modules). Only the latest revision of each design is shown.
- **Columns** — Project phases (or batches, depending on the view).
- **Cells** — The quantity count for each design × phase combination.
- **Totals** — Row totals (all phases for a design) and column totals (all designs in a phase).

## View Modes

Two buttons in the toolbar switch the axis: **Phases** shows the project phases, **Batches** shows the batches of one phase, picked in the selector beside them. The choice is kept in the address bar, so a reload or Back keeps you where you were, and a phase view can be bookmarked or shared.

### Phase View

Shows a high-level summary with one column per project phase. Each cell shows the total quantity of a design across all batches in that phase.

### Batch View

Select a specific phase to drill down into its batches. Each column represents a batch, showing the detailed quantity breakdown.

## Managing Quantities

- **Edit cells** — The **−** / **+** buttons appear on the cell you point at, and on the cell you select. Click the number, or just start typing, to enter one. Only whole numbers of zero or more are accepted.
- **Add phase** — Create a new project phase. You can optionally pick a phase template (see below) to pre-fill its batches.
- **Add batch** — Create a new batch within a phase.
- **Delete phase/batch** — Remove from the project.
- **Load from project** — Restore previously saved quantities.
- **Reset** — Recalculate the matrix from the units that already exist. This also deletes the quantities saved on the project, so it asks for confirmation first.

Quantities are **saved automatically** a couple of seconds after you stop editing. The toolbar shows *Unsaved*, *Saving…* or *Saved*, with a Save button while there is anything pending, and it also saves when you leave the view.

### Saved is not the same as generated

*Saved* means your numbers are stored on the project. It does not mean the panels exist: the matrix is a plan, and the units are only created or deleted when you press **Generate**.

So the **Generate** button says whether the two agree:

- When they do not, it is filled and carries the difference — `Generate  +42 / −3`, units to create and units to delete. Hover it for the detail.
- When they do, it is drawn quietly, because pressing it would change nothing.

There are two ways to make them agree:

- **Generate** — create and delete units so production follows the matrix.
- **Bulk → Reset quantities to the existing units** — discard the numbers and read them back from the units that exist.

The numbers on the button are what **Generate** would actually do, so a difference it reports is always a difference you can act on.

### Keyboard

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| Arrow keys | move between cells |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> / <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Tab</kbd> | next / previous column |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> / <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Enter</kbd> | next / previous row |
| type a digit, or <kbd>F2</kbd> | overwrite the value |
| <kbd>+</kbd> / <kbd>−</kbd> | step the value by one |
| <kbd>Delete</kbd> | set to zero |
| <kbd>Esc</kbd> | cancel editing, or clear the selection |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>D</kbd> | copy the selected value down the column |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>V</kbd> | paste a column of numbers copied from Excel |
| <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Z</kbd> / <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Y</kbd> | undo / redo |

A fill-down, a paste, *Set multiple numbers* or *Auto-allocate by prefix* all undo in a single step. The **?** button in the toolbar lists all of this.

### Reading the matrix

The second column shows **assigned / target** for each design, frozen next to the design name. It turns green when the two match and amber (or red, in the batch view) when they do not — that is the number to watch while filling the matrix.

Above the matrix, a status bar totals the project: target, assigned, area, and how many designs do not add up. Hover the **target** figure to see which IFC file each part of it came from.

### Where the target comes from

The target is the number of units the IFC splitter found for each design. It is worked out from the splitter's own counts, so it updates by itself every time you split a file.

Three actions in the **Bulk** menu, under *Project totals*:

- **Clear the project totals** — empties the targets. The splitter counts themselves are kept, so this is reversible.
- **Recover totals** — rebuilds the targets from every piece of splitter information available. It shows each design, where its number comes from, and what would change, before writing anything. The matrix is not touched.
- **Set totals into the matrix** — writes each design's project total into the phase columns.

Under *Project matrix* are the actions that change your plan rather than the targets: **Load numbers from project splitter** and **Recalculate from existing units**.

If **Recover totals** finds nothing, this project has no splitter counts stored — split the IFC again to rebuild them.

#### Projects without targets

A project you never split has no targets, and neither does a design you added by hand. Those rows show only the number you assigned: no target, no colour, no balance button, and they are not counted as not adding up. The status bar drops the target figure too. Nothing to compare against, nothing claimed.

The same applies per design, so a project where only some designs came from a split judges those and leaves the rest alone.

### Balancing

- **Balance a row** — an unbalanced row has a button next to its assigned/target figure. It spreads the difference over the columns that already carry a number, keeping their proportions. If the row has nothing allocated yet, it all goes on the first column.
- **Balance all** — in the status bar. It shows which designs it will change, and by how much, before you commit.

When a phase has many batches the matrix scrolls sideways. The design name and the target/assigned column stay frozen on the left, the header row stays on top, and the grand total stays pinned at the bottom.

## Phase templates and automation

These tools speed up setting up a phase and filling its batches. The buttons appear in the matrix toolbar when a phase (batch view) is selected.

### Phase templates

A phase template is a reusable set of batches, defined once per company. Each batch in the template has a name and an optional list of **name prefixes** and a production line.

Templates are managed in **Projects Settings → Phase templates**, in an expandable section at the bottom of the page, and are available to all the projects of the company. When you create a phase, choosing a template automatically creates its batches in that phase, including their prefixes.

A phase created from a template shows a ✨ icon next to its name. Open the phase menu and choose **Set phase template** to see which template is applied or to apply a different one — its batches are created or updated to match.

### Batch prefixes

Each batch can carry the name prefixes used for auto-numbering. A batch with prefixes shows a split icon next to its name. Open the batch menu and choose **Prefixes** to view or edit them. Templates fill these in automatically, but you can adjust them per batch at any time.

### Add panels for module counts

In the **phase view**, set how many of each module you want in a phase, then click **Add panels for module counts**. The panels each module contains are taken from the module's own parsed contents and set on the same phase, multiplied by the module count. This works whether you used the project splitter or only the module splitter.

A dialog asks whether to set the numbers in batches too:

- **Also batches** — set the phase totals and also distribute them into the phase's batches by prefix (so you can generate right away).
- **Only phases** — set just the phase totals and leave the batches untouched.
- **Close** — do nothing.

The panel totals are recalculated from the module counts each time, so clicking the button again does not double the counts.

Hover the tree icon next to a module's name to see its decomposition — the panel (assembly) design names and how many of each the module contains.

### Auto-allocate by prefix

In the **batch view** (with a phase selected), click **Auto-allocate by prefix** to send each design's phase number into the batch whose prefix matches the design name. When a name matches several prefixes, the longest (most specific) prefix wins. Designs that match no batch are reported and left unassigned.

Together these give a simple flow: place module numbers on a phase → add the panels for those modules → switch to the phase's batches and auto-allocate by prefix → generate.

## Generating Constructibles

Once your quantities are defined, click **Generate Constructibles** to create the actual assembly and module instances based on the matrix counts.

The dialog shows how many units will be created and how many deleted before you commit.

::: warning
For every design, the batch quantities of a phase must add up to that phase's quantity. If they do not, the dialog lists exactly which designs and phases are off and by how much, and generation is blocked until you fix them.
:::

Your saved quantities are only cleared once the units have actually been created. If generation fails, they are kept and you can retry.

Quantities are saved against the designs and batches you wrote them for. If any of those are deleted afterwards, their numbers can no longer be generated, and the dialog lists them as outdated quantities that will be discarded. Pressing **Generate** drops them and creates the rest.

## Area Metrics

Toggle the area display to see total square meters alongside quantity counts. This helps estimate material requirements and production workload.
