# Issues Management

The Issues view provides a centralized overview of all production issues and quality control records across a project.

<!-- TODO: screenshot of the issues management view with summary and table -->

[[toc]]

## Overview

At the top, a summary card shows:

- Total issue count
- Breakdown by category: **Quality Control** issues and **Production Issues**

Below the summary, a data table lists all issues with their details.

## Issue Categories

| Category | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| **Quality Control** | Issues related to product quality, compliance, or inspection findings. |
| **Production Issue** | Problems encountered during the manufacturing process (delays, equipment, material defects). |

## Issue Fields

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Title** | Short description of the issue. |
| **Description** | Detailed explanation of the problem. |
| **Category** | Quality control or production issue. |
| **Constructible** | The assembly or module affected. |
| **Created by** | The user who reported the issue. |
| **Created at** | When the issue was reported. |
| **Status** | Open or solved. |
| **Pictures** | Optional photos or screenshots attached to the issue. |

## Creating Issues

Issues can be created from two places:

1. **Issues view** — Click the create button to add a new issue to any constructible.
2. **3D Viewer** — While viewing a constructible, click the issues button to report a problem directly from the production floor. You can attach the current part information for context.

## Resolving Issues

To close an issue:

1. Open the issue detail.
2. Mark it as **solved**.
3. Add a resolution comment explaining how it was fixed.

::: info
Issues on design templates can be solved with a new design revision, which applies the fix to all future instances of that design.
:::

## Filtering

Use the table controls to filter issues by:

- Category (quality control / production issue)
- Status (open / solved)
- User
- Date range

pages.body:
# Reports

Reports let you generate documents from your project data — Bills of Materials, production spreadsheets, QR stickers, quality control PDFs, and more.

<!-- TODO: screenshot of the reports table showing a list of generated reports -->

[[toc]]

## Creating a Report

1. Go to **Production files** (machine files and shop-floor documents) or **Management files** (office documents). Both exist inside a project and company-wide, under the Files section of the menu.
2. Click the **New Report** button.
3. In the report form dialog:
   - Select the **document type** (e.g., Plates BoM, Production Excel).
   - Choose which **assemblies or modules** to include.
   - Configure any **options** specific to the report type.
4. Click **Submit** to queue the report for generation.

<!-- TODO: screenshot of the report form dialog -->

::: tip
You can also click **Save Without Generating** to create the report entry without starting generation. This is useful if you want to configure the report now and generate it later.
:::

## File Defaults

Each document type has a set of options — cover page, how parts are grouped, table style, paper size, and so on. **File settings** lets you set what those options start at, per type, for the whole company.

Open **File settings** in the Files section of the company menu, expand **File defaults**, and pick a type. The form is the same one you see when creating the file. Save, and every new file of that type starts from your values.

- A type with nothing saved shows **System defaults** and uses the values built into Produuz.it.
- A type you have configured shows **Custom defaults**. **Reset** puts it back to the system values.
- Files already created keep the settings they were saved with. Changing a default never changes a document you generated earlier.
- Files generated from a template use these defaults too.

**Machine files are not in this list.** Their options depend on the machine model, so their defaults live on the machine setup, in Production stations.

## Generation Templates

A generation template is a saved set of files you always create together — for example a Plates BoM, a Wood BoM and the QR stickers for the same panels. Instead of filling the report form three times, you pick the template, select the panels once, and every file in it is queued in one action.

Templates are managed in **File settings**, under the Files section of the company menu. Each file in a template is one document type, plus the machine or production line it should use when the type needs one.

To use one, click **Run template** in Production files or Management files, choose the template, select the panels and click **Generate**. You can also create a template on the spot from that same dialog.

## Report Status

Once submitted, a report goes through these stages:

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **Waiting** | Queued for processing |
| **Working** | Being generated (progress percentage shown) |
| **Ready** | Successfully generated — click to download |
| **Failed** | An error occurred during generation |

When a report fails, you'll receive an email notification.

## Versioning

Each time you regenerate a report, a new version is created. All previous versions are kept and can be downloaded from the version history.

::: info Design Updates
If a design's IFC file is updated after a report was generated, a warning icon will appear next to the report. This means the report may contain outdated data. You can regenerate it to include the latest design changes.
:::

## Content Selection

Most reports require you to select which content to include:

- **Assemblies / Modules** — Select specific items from the project tree.
- **Part Batches** — Some reports allow selecting by part batch instead, which groups parts across assemblies.

## Project Reports vs. Company Reports

**Project reports** are generated from a specific project's data. Most report types are project-scoped, including all Bills of Materials and machine files.

**Company reports** are available when you need data across all projects. These include:
- Production Excel
- Worktime Excel
- Quality Control Report
- Issues Report

Company reports use a **date range** filter instead of content selection, and can optionally be filtered by production line.

## Report Types

### Bills of Materials

PDF documents listing the parts needed for your constructibles:

- [**Plates BoM**](/guide/reports/plates_bom/) — All plate parts with quantities and dimensions.
- [**Wood BoM**](/guide/reports/wood_bom/) — All wood/profile parts.
- [**Per-Design BoM**](/guide/reports/designs_bom/) — One BoM per unique design.
- [**Accessories BoM**](/guide/reports/accesories_bom/) — Accessories and hardware list.
- [**Custom Woods CSV**](/guide/reports/custom_woodcsv/) — Wood parts exported as CSV.
- [**Custom Plates CSV**](/guide/reports/custom_platecsv/) — Plate parts exported as CSV.
- [**Custom Accessories CSV**](/guide/reports/custom_accesorycsv/) — Accessories exported as CSV.

### Project Reports

- [**Production Excel**](/guide/reports/production_excel/) — Production planning spreadsheet.
- [**Worktime Excel**](/guide/reports/worktime_excel/) — Worker time tracking spreadsheet.
- [**Quality Control Report**](/guide/reports/quality_control/) — PDF summarizing quality control records.
- [**Issues Report**](/guide/reports/issues/) — PDF listing all issues found during production.
- [**QR Stickers**](/guide/reports/qr_stickers/) — Printable QR code labels for physical identification.

### Machine Files

Machine-specific file formats for CNC equipment. See the [Machine Files](/guide/machine_files/formats/panel_mob1/) section for details.

pages.body:
# Wood BoM

The Wood Bill of Materials generates a PDF document listing all wood and profile parts for your selected constructibles.

<!-- TODO: screenshot of a Wood BoM PDF output -->

## Output

- **Format:** PDF (single file or ZIP with multiple PDFs)
- **Content:** All wood/profile parts with dimensions, quantities, materials, and optional cross-section drawings.

## Options

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Grouping** | Choose how parts are organized: all in one document, grouped by batch, or one per assembly. |
| **Cover page** | Include a title page with project information. |
| **Designs summary** | Add a summary table listing all included designs. |
| **Materials totals page** | Append a page with total material quantities (linear meters per material type). |
| **Show profile side drawings** | Include wood profile cross-section drawings. |
| **Group parts that differ only in length** | On by default. Parts with the same details and a different length share one table and one drawing, with the length shown as LENGTH. See [below](#parts-that-differ-only-in-length). |
| **Cross-section filter** | Filter by specific cross-section types. |
| **Table style** | Choose between "Extended tables" or "Classic tables" layout. |
| **Combine** | When grouping by batch or assembly, merge all PDFs into one combined file. |
| **Attach to viewer** | Link the generated PDF to the assembly in the 3D Viewer. |
| **Filter by material** | Only include wood parts of specific material types. |

## Parts that differ only in length

With **Show profile side drawings** on, each wood part with a detail (a drilling, a notch, an angled end cut) gets a table and a drawing of its own. When several parts have exactly the same details and differ only in their length — the studs of a sloped wall, all with the same angled top cut — they now share **one table and one drawing**, with a row per part.

- The drawing shows the length as **LENGTH**, with no number. The real length of each part is in its row.
- The part of the length that changes is drawn short, between two break marks.
- Details before it are measured from the left end, below the drawing. Details after it are measured from the right end, above the drawing, each end with its own 0.
- Only the length may differ: a different width, height, section, material, finish or comment keeps the parts apart. Details must match within 1 mm.
- A part turned end for end or turned over counts as the same part. A mirrored part does not.
- A group has **one** changing length or none. If some parts change before a detail and others after it, they form separate groups.

Turn it off with **Group parts that differ only in length** to get one table per part again. The drawing of each part, in the viewer and in logistics, is not affected: it keeps all its numbers.

## Grouping Modes

- **Selected** — One single PDF with all selected content.
- **Batch** — One PDF per batch (ZIP output).
- **Panels** — One PDF per assembly (ZIP output).

## Parts that differ only in length

With **Show profile side drawings** on, each wood part with a detail (a drilling, a notch, an angled end cut) gets a table and a drawing of its own. When several parts have exactly the same details and differ only in their length — the studs of a sloped wall, all with the same angled top cut — they now share **one table and one drawing**, with a row per part.

- The drawing shows the length as **LENGTH**, with no number. The real length of each part is in its row.
- The part of the length that changes is drawn short, between two break marks.
- Details before it are measured from the left end, below the drawing. Details after it are measured from the right end, above the drawing, each end with its own 0.

## When to Use

This report type is ideal when you want a complete BoM per design type rather than per physical assembly. Useful for purchasing and material planning where quantities are calculated per design variant.

pages.title: MOB v1 Machine File
pages.body:
# MOB v1 Machine File

The MOB v1 is a text-based machine file format used to send manufacturing instructions to automated timber wall panel processing machines like the Mobi One.

<!-- TODO: screenshot of a MOB file being generated in the reports dialog -->

[[toc]]

## What It Contains

A MOB v1 file describes all the operations needed to process a wall panel. It is organized into **layers** (representing different faces/sides of the panel), each containing a sequence of **operation commands**.

### Layers

Each layer represents a work zone on the panel:

- **Inside layers** — The inner face of the panel.
- **Center/wood layers** — The framing structure (studs, plates).
- **Outside layers** — The outer face of the panel.

### Operation Types

| Operation | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| **Framing** | Beam cuts, angle cuts, vertical and horizontal cuts for frame members. |
| **Nailing** | Line nailing patterns with configurable spacing for fastening cladding and battens. |
| **Plate positioning** | Cladding plate placement coordinates. |
| **Milling** | Routing paths, circles, and ellipses for openings and cutouts. |
| **Sawing** | Transverse cuts across the panel. |
| **Drilling** | Hole positions for connections and hardware. |
| **Gluing** | Adhesive application lines for bonding. |

## File Structure

The MOB file is plain text with semicolon-terminated command rows:

```
VERSION 3.00;
TXT # MOB Conversion by Produuz.it;
REIHE inside;
ELN DesignName;
ELM max_x, max_y, height, scale, 0, 0;
Layer [zone details];
[operation commands]
End Layer;
```

Each command has a code (e.g., `NRZ`, `BR`, `PSG`) followed by numeric parameters defining positions, dimensions, and tool settings.

## Generation Options

When generating MOB v1 files, you can configure:

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Starting side** | Begin processing from the inside or outside face. |
| **Shift mode** | How operations are shifted between layers (none, by layer, by operation). |
| **Nailing pattern** | Regular, large panel, or optimized nail placement. |
| **CTC spacing** | Center-to-center distance for nail lines. |
| **Mill direction** | Clockwise or counter-clockwise per zone. |
| **Tool assignments** | Which nailer, saw, or mill unit to use per zone. |
| **Operation trimming** | Automatically trim operations that exceed machine limits. |

## Output

- **Format:** ZIP containing one `.mob` file per assembly
- **Requires:** A production line with a configured machine (e.g., Mobi One)

## MOB v1 vs. MOB v2

| | MOB v1 | MOB v2 |
|---|--------|--------|
| **Machine** | Mobi One V1 | Mobi One V2 |
| **Carriages** | Single carriage | Dual carriages (left + right) |
| **Flooring** | Not supported | Multi-station flooring operations |
| **Tool control** | Basic tool selection | Granular per-carriage tool zones |
| **Complexity** | Simpler, widely used | More advanced, newer installations |

pages.title: BTL File
pages.body:
# BTL File (Wood Profiles)

The BTL format generates cutting instructions for wood profile processing machines. It's used by Hundegger and H&M Truss Master equipment for cutting studs, beams, and other timber members.

[[toc]]

## Output

- **Format:** ZIP containing `.btl` files
- **Target machines:** H&M Truss Master, Hundegger Speed-Cut, Hundegger Turbo-Drive

## Parameters

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| **Group parts** | How to organize output files: 'By Panel', 'By Batch', or 'By Phase'. | By Panel |
| **Split shared references per panel** | Only when grouping By Batch or By Phase. Keeps a reference that appears in several panels as one entry **per panel** — each with its own quantity and its own panel fields — instead of merging them into a single line. Example: `P50` used 3× in one panel and 2× in another produces two entries (count 3 and count 2). | Off |
| **Split by sizes** | Create separate files for each profile size. | Off |
| **Create marks** | Add marks/labels on processed parts. | Off |
| **Angle decimal places** | Number of decimal places for angle values. | 1 |
| **Filter parts by prefix** | Only include parts whose reference starts with specific prefixes. | — |

### Part data fields

The standard "Part data" fields that your machine/SCM software reads — **Designation, Assembly number, Group, Package, Material, Timber grade, Quality grade** and **Subgroup / Storey** — can now be filled with whatever you want, per machine. Each field is a small template where you type free text and/or **properties** wrapped in curly braces (see below). This lets you export a whole **batch or phase** in a single file while every part still carries its own panel identity, instead of having to export panel by panel.

For example, setting **Designation** to `{part_pos} ; {assembly_name}` produces values like `5461 ; HD-529`.

The defaults reproduce the previous behaviour, so nothing changes until you edit a field. These fields apply to the BTL and BTLx files (not to the panel-frame BTL).

### User Attributes

You can define up to 5 custom attributes that are embedded in the BTL file. Each has a **name** and **value** field. Use these to pass additional metadata to your machine software.

### Properties

Both the part data fields and the user attribute values accept **properties** in curly braces, replaced per part — `{part_pos}`, `{assembly_name}`, `{material}`, `{batch}`, your own model properties, and so on. Each field has an **Insert property** button listing everything it accepts.

The full list, the rules and where else properties work: **[Properties in texts](/guide/properties/)**.

# Frame Nailer CSV

The Frame Nailer format generates nailing operation lists for H&M frame nailer machines.

[[toc]]

## Output

- **Format:** ZIP containing `.csv` files
- **Target machines:** H&M Frame Nailer

## File Contents

Each CSV contains nailing patterns and positions for frame assembly, mapping beams to nail positions based on beam dimensions.

## Parameters

### Framing Nailing Matrix

Define the nailing pattern based on beam size:

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Beam size (mm)** | Width of the beam. |
| **Top padding (mm)** | Distance from the top edge to the first nail. |
| **Bottom padding (mm)** | Distance from the bottom edge to the last nail. |
| **Number of nails** | How many nails per beam at this size. |

### Nailing matrix rows are size ranges

Off by default: each row applies to the exact beam size written in it, and a
size that is not in the matrix gets the automatic nailing.

Turn it on and every row becomes the **start of a size range** that runs up to
the next row, with the last row covering everything above it. A matrix with
rows at 89, 120 and 160 then nails 89-119 with the first row, 120-159 with the
second and 160 and up with the third, so you no longer need one row per
millimetre. Sizes below the first row stay outside the matrix.

pages.title: Mobi One
pages.body:
# Mobi One

The Mobi One (by H&M) is an automated timber wall panel processing machine. It handles the entire panel manufacturing process — framing, nailing, milling, sawing, drilling, and gluing — in a single station.

<!-- TODO: screenshot of the Mobi One machine configuration in produuz.it -->

[[toc]]

## Overview

The Mobi One is set up as a **machine** linked to a **station** in your production line. When a constructible reaches that station, the system can generate MOB machine files with all the manufacturing instructions.

There are two versions:
- **Mobi One V1** — Single-carriage design, generates MOB v1 files.
- **Mobi One V2** — Dual-carriage design with expanded capabilities, generates MOB v2 files.

## Processing Units

The Mobi One can be equipped with various processing units depending on your configuration:

| Unit | Function |
|------|----------|
| **Framing** | Processes frame members (studs, top/bottom plates) |
| **Nailers** | High-speed pneumatic nailers for fastening cladding and battens |
| **Screwers** | Mechanical screw drivers |
| **Miller/Router** | Spindle for routing openings, cutouts, and milling operations |
| **Drill** | Multi-spindle or single-head drilling |
| **Saw** | Cross-cutting blade for transverse cuts |
| **Gluing** | Adhesive application system |

## Configuration in Produuz.it

### Machine Setup

In **Company Settings > Production Lines**, configure the Mobi One with:

- **Layer orientation** — Inside, outside, or none.
- **X-axis mirroring** — Mirror operations along the X-axis if needed.
- **Machine zero position** — The reference point for the coordinate system (top-right, top-left, bottom-right, or bottom-left).
- **Nailing matrix** — Customize nail patterns by beam size. Each beam size row sets the top/bottom padding and the number of nails. The beam size is the height of the stud where it meets the rail. Rows are kept sorted by beam size when the setup is saved.
- **Nailing matrices by part class** — The matrix window can hold one whole matrix per **part class**: the matrix by beam size, the nail columns by beam width and their two range switches, all of them per class. Pick **Default** or a class at the top of the window; add a class with the field beside it, choosing one of the classes of your parsing setups or typing a new name. A stud whose class has a matrix is nailed by it; a size or width with no row in that matrix falls back to the default matrix, and then to the automatic nailing. This is how a panel that mixes I-beams and solid studs of the same height gets two nails on the I-beams and five on the studs. See: [IFC Parsing Setup](/guide/management/ifcps/)
- **Nail columns by beam width** — Next to the matrix, a second table decides how many **columns of nails** a stud gets from its width: set *No of Columns* to 2 or more and *Column Spacing* to the horizontal distance between columns, per beam width. The machine file then repeats the nail row at each extra column position. A width that is not in the table gets a single column. Its rows can also be read as width ranges with **Nail columns rows are width ranges**, exactly like the size ranges of the matrix, and they are kept sorted by width as well. The window that holds both tables shows a **preview**: type a beam height and width and it draws the stud's joint with the nails the machine would drive, saying which matrix row or range answered, or that the automatic nailing applies, and warning when a column would fall outside the stud. The columns are drawn where the machine drives them: the first one 22 mm from the stud's edge (the nailer's offset from the X written in the file, which centres it on a 44 mm stud), the next ones one spacing further each.
- **Nailing matrix rows are size ranges** — Off by default, so each row applies to the exact beam size written in it. When on, every row is the start of a size range that runs up to the next row (the last row covers everything above it): rows at 89, 120 and 160 nail 89-119, 120-159 and 160 and up, instead of needing one row per millimetre. Sizes below the first row stay outside the matrix and get the automatic nailing.
- **Processing thresholds** — Minimum mill radius, CTC distances, and other tolerances.
- **Treat extra woods as normal frame woods** — Off by default. When off, extra woods (extra top/bottom wood and extra frame wood profiles) are handled as reinforcements: the extra rails are placed as ordinary horizontal pieces and get ledge nailing. When on, they are handled exactly like the rest of the frame: extra rails become top/bottom rails, they are nailed with the standard framing matrix, and they are included in flooring.
- **Angular nailing** — Off by default. For machines equipped with a tilting nailer unit: nailer codes in the file are written with 4 digits (`00`, `10` or `20` in front of the tool number). Nailing along the panel contour, around windows and in the middle of a plate stays straight (`00` + tool). At a joint between two plates, the nail row on the left side of the joint gets `10` + tool and the one on the right side gets `20` + tool, so each row is driven at an angle into the shared wood. Every zone also gets a **Nail Context** drawing with the operation drawings, showing how each nail line was classified (contour, window, plate joint or plate face).
- **SVG Drawings** — All on by default. One switch per operation drawing generated with the machine files: Framing nails, Frame Glueing, Operations (plates nailing), Glueing, Bricks, Isolation, Battens, Batten Intersections, Plates Layout and the Nail Context debug drawing. Turn off the ones you don't use to skip generating them — the machine files themselves are not affected. In a production line with several stations, the switches of the machine that owns zone 0 (the frame) apply to the whole line.

::: info
This option is set **per station**, so each machine in the production line decides on its own. The typical use is a line where the frame station builds the frame without the extra pieces (option off) and a later station receives the panel with them already mounted (option on).

A station with the option on also measures the panel from a different corner: because the extra pieces are already mounted, the panel is physically bigger, so its zero is the corner of the frame *including* them. Stations with the option off keep measuring from the structural frame, and an extra piece that sticks out lands on negative coordinates — the same as before.
:::

### Job Settings

When generating machine files, configure per-job options:

- **Starting side** — Which face to begin processing (inside or outside).
- **Shift mode** — How operations are shifted between layers.
- **Nailing pattern** — Regular, large panel, or optimized.
- **Mill direction** — Clockwise or counter-clockwise per zone.
- **Tool assignments** — Which physical unit to use for each zone.
- **CTC spacing** — Center-to-center distances for nail lines.

::: info
Job settings can be saved as defaults on the machine setup, so you don't have to configure them each time you generate files.
:::

## Generating Machine Files

1. Go to the **Reports** tab in your project.
2. Click **New Report** and select **MOB v1 Machine File** (or MOB v2).
3. Select the assemblies to process.
4. Choose the production line and machine.
5. Adjust job settings if needed.
6. Click **Submit** to generate.

The output is a ZIP file containing one `.mob` file per assembly.

## Linking to Production

When the Mobi One station is configured in your production line, the machine files are available to production workers through the [Viewer](/guide/viewer/). The operations drawings button shows the machine processing sequence for each constructible.

pages.title: Frame Station
pages.body:
# Frame Station

The **Frame Station** is a machine type dedicated to the **frame layer** (zone 0) of a wall or floor panel — the structural frame of studs and top/bottom rails, before any cladding goes on.

[[toc]]

## Why a dedicated machine type

On most lines the frame is built on a Mobi One that also handles the cladding faces. Reusing that machine for the frame meant carrying a lot of settings that don't apply to the frame, and — more importantly — it forced the **inside** and **outside** faces of the frame to share a single configuration.

The Frame Station solves this:

- It only exposes the settings that are relevant to the frame layer (framing nails matrix, frame gluing, machine zero, etc.).
- It lets you configure the **inside** and **outside** faces **independently**, using `_in` / `_out` options.

It comes in two versions, matching Mobi One:

- **Frame Station V1** — produces **MOB v1** machine files.
- **Frame Station V2** — produces **MOB v2** machine files.

Both accept a machine configuration file upload, just like the Mobi One machines.

## Configuration in Produuz.it

In **Company Settings > Production Lines**, add a station with a machine of type **Frame Station** and assign it zone **0**.

### Machine settings

- **General** — Machine zero, blocker heights, max wall length. (No generic direction switches here — orientation is set per face under **Face Inversion**.)
- **Framing** — Auto framing nail matrix paddings and minimum CtC, dynamic nail positioning, clamp deactivation. The **Nailing matrix by beam size** opens in its own window from here: the matrix by beam size (height), with the option to read its rows as size ranges (each row covers from its own size up to the next one) instead of exact sizes, and the table of **nail columns by beam width**, with its own ranges option. Both tables are kept sorted when the setup is saved.
- **Face Inversion (per face, per axis):** whether each whole face of the frame is machined flipped. When enabled, **all** of that face's operations — woods, nailing, sawing, drilling, flooring and glue — are mirrored on the chosen axis. X and Y are independent and set per face:
  - **Invert X axis (outside face)** / **Invert Y axis (outside face)**
  - **Invert X axis (inside face)** / **Invert Y axis (inside face)**

::: info
The inversion is applied at the geometry level (the face is read from the matching wrapper/origin), so the whole face stays consistent — it is not a per-operation tweak. It never affects the layer stacking (Z).
:::

## When to enable the face inversions

If the two faces of the frame are machined in opposite orientations and one face (typically the **outside**) comes out mirrored relative to the other, enable the X and/or Y inversion for that face. The whole face then follows the orientation the machine uses to machine it.

pages.title: Logistics
pages.body:
# Logistics

The Logistics view provides an overview of material requirements across your constructibles, helping you track which parts are available and which still need to be prepared.

<!-- TODO: screenshot of the logistics view showing material inventory table -->

[[toc]]

## Layout

The screen is laid out like the panel viewer:

- **The table**, with the branch and size pickers above it. Nothing else — what
  chooses the list stays with the list.
- **The toolbar**, a column beside it, holding the part batch, the search, the
  sorting, the columns, *Set all parts ready* and every message the view has to
  give you.
- **The part panel**, showing the drawing and the properties of the part you
  picked in the table.

The top button in the toolbar opens and closes the part panel: with it closed
the table takes the whole width. The choice is remembered on the device.

On a phone the toolbar becomes a bar at the bottom of the screen; press the
chevron and it opens upwards.

## Material Tracking

The table shows each material part needed for production, organized by:

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Zone** | The structural area in the design where this part is used. Projects without zones don't show this column. |
| **Reference** | Material identification code. |
| **Material** | Material name. |
| **Dimensions** | Width and length (for plates) or length (for profiles). |
| **Total** | Total number of this part needed across all constructibles. |
| **Pending** | How many are still to be prepared. |
| **% ready** | Progress of the row. |
| **Constructibles** | Breakdown showing how many are needed for each assembly/module. Long lists are cut to three, with the rest behind a `+N` chip. |
| **Ready parts** | How many have been prepared and are available. |

A totals line at the bottom sums up rows, parts, ready, pending and the overall percentage.

## Sorting

Click any column header to sort by it, and shift-click a second header to sort by
both. Zone and reference sort naturally, so `Z2` comes before `Z10` and reference
`9` before `114`.

The **Sort** menu has four ready-made orders:

- **Longest first** — the default, for cutting at the saw.
- **Reference A-Z** — to find a specific part.
- **Pending first** — to see what is still missing.
- **Zone then reference** — the kitting order.

The same menu switches between **Group by zone**, where each zone is a header row
with its own progress and the sorting applies inside it, and **Flat list**, where
the order applies to the whole table. Projects without zones always use the flat
list.

Your sorting, grouping, density and hidden columns are remembered on the device.

## Filtering

- **Branch** — Switch between viewing plate materials or profile materials.
- **Size** — Filter to a specific material size. One at a time: this is a
  production view, and a run at the saw is one size.
- **Search** — Filter the table by reference, zone or material.
- **Hide completed** — Leave only the rows with parts still pending.

## Columns

The table only shows columns that say something different on each row. When
every part in the list is the same material — which is what usually happens,
since you pick a branch and a size before the list appears — the **Material**
column is dropped and the material is written once above the table, as a chip.
The same goes for **Finish**, **Comment** and, on plates, **Width**.

Columns you can turn on and off yourself are in the **Columns** menu, together
with the row density.

## Selecting from a Report

Above the panel list, **Select from report** takes the selection of a report and
loads it into the menu: pick one and the assemblies and modules it has selected
are ticked for you.

Only reports marked as **final** are listed — a document still being worked on is
not something to produce against — so the button is not there at all when the
project has no final report yet.

## Part Batches

A part batch is a run of work: the parts you are about to cut, from the moment
you start until you finish and put the leftover material back.

The **batch block** sits at the top of the toolbar:

1. **Pick a batch** in the selector, if somebody prepared one for you in the
   parts list. Picking it makes the table show that batch and nothing else.
2. **Start production** — with no batch picked, this creates one out of what is
   on the table (your selection, the branch and the size) and starts it.
   **Start batch** does the same for the batch you picked. Either way, who
   started it and when are recorded, and from then on the counters work.
   Before that, the counters are locked and *Set all parts ready* is not there.
   If those parts are already in a batch that has been started, that batch is
   opened and resumed instead of a second one being started over the same
   work — one press, whether it was left running or paused.
3. **While it runs**, the bar shows the progress of the whole batch and the time
   worked. **Pause** stops the clock; the counters lock again until you resume.
4. **Finish batch** — or marking the last pending part — opens the form for the
   material that goes back to stock.

Several batches can run at the same time, and you can switch between them
whenever you want. If you leave a running batch — by picking another one, by
changing the selection, or by navigating away — you are asked whether to pause
the one you are leaving, exactly like leaving a panel with an open checklist in
the viewer.

Nothing happens automatically overnight: a batch stays open until somebody
pauses or finishes it.

### Material returned to stock

The closing form asks only for what **comes back**, in the units you buy it in:

- **Returned whole** — bars or sheets that go back unopened.
- **Remnants** — the usable offcuts, with their length (and width, for sheets).
- **Scrap** — what is thrown away.
- **Rack** — where you leave it, and a free notes field.

If the bar length or sheet size you used is not in the list, type it and it is
added to your product catalogue, so next time it is already there.

Closing with **Nothing to return** is a normal outcome and needs no explanation.

Produuz.it does not keep stock levels: this declaration is sent onwards, to the
system that does.

### Where the batches live

**Part batches** lists them all: status, production line, project, progress,
start, finish, time worked and who ran them. Clicking the name opens a panel on
the right with the batch in full — its parts, its work sessions and the material
declared as returned — and the buttons to open it in the logistics view, pause or
resume it, finish it and reopen it.

The view is in two places: in the **company menu**, where it lists every batch of
the company, and in the **project menu**, where it lists only the batches of that
project and drops the project column. Switching between All projects and a
project keeps you on the list.

The **production line** is changed from that panel. It is the only field of a
batch you can edit there, and it is saved as soon as you pick it.

Batches can also be composed by hand from the **Parts list**, by
selecting parts and assigning them to a batch. That is the place to build a
batch that mixes several sizes: the logistics view always works on one size at
a time.

## Marking Parts Ready

You can update the "ready parts" count for each material to track preparation progress:

- Click on the number to type it, or use the `−` and `+` buttons.
- Use the **Set all parts ready** button to mark everything currently listed as
  ready. It asks for confirmation first. Without a batch it only affects the rows
  you can see — so searching or hiding completed rows narrows it down — while with
  a batch running it marks the whole batch, and says so.

## Kitted Parts

A **kit** is everything a panel is built from. While its parts are still being cut,
the panel cannot be assembled — and the production list now says so.

### What production sees

On the panel list in the viewer, each panel carries one label:

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **13 parts left** | still being cut. Grey while nothing has been cut yet, amber once cutting has started |
| **Kitted parts** | every part is ready — this panel can be built |
| *(station marks)* | work has started; the station marks carry the row from here |
| **Ready** | the panel is built |

There is only ever one label. A panel with no parts recorded shows none, because
there is nothing to report about a kit that does not exist. If a panel is started
while parts are still missing, the count stays on the row in red.

### Where the count comes from

A panel is kitted when **all of its parts are marked ready** in the logistics
table. Parts that were replaced by a newer revision do not count — they are no
longer part of the panel.

A **module** is kitted when every panel it contains has been **built**, and its own
loose parts are ready. A module cannot be assembled until its panels physically
exist, so a panel that merely has a complete kit is not enough.

### Choosing who decides

**Company settings → Kitted parts** has three options:

| Option | Who decides |
|---|---|
| **Off** | nobody. Nothing about kits is shown anywhere |
| **Manual** | the logistics operator marks a panel kitted by hand |
| **Automatic** *(recommended)* | the ready counts decide, on their own |

On **Manual**, two things appear:

- when every part of a panel you have selected becomes ready, a line appears above
  the logistics table naming those panels, with a button to mark them;
- every panel in the logistics menu shows its kit progress, with a tick beside it
  to mark that one panel. Use this when you know the kit is fine even though the
  counts disagree — an offcut used, a part cut outside the flow.

Marking a kit by hand never changes a panel's production status.

### Starting a panel that is not ready

If you start a panel whose parts are not all cut, the viewer says so and tells you how many
are missing. **You can always carry on** — it is a warning, not a block. It appears once,
when the panel is started, and not again when you move to the next station.

### In the Constructibles list

The Constructibles list gains a **Kit** column
showing the same thing as a fraction — `12/25`, `✓ 25/25`, or `—` when the panel has
no parts. It sorts, so you can put the panels closest to ready at the top.

### On the dashboard

**Ready to build** shows everything still to be built, per production line, split into
what can be built now, what is partly cut, what has not been cut yet, and what has no parts
recorded at all. The big number on top is what your factory could start today.

It sits next to **Active backlog**, which answers a different question: that one says where
your panels are in production, this one says whether their material is there. A line with
forty panels waiting and five kits complete has a material problem, not a production one.

## Part Drawings

When a part is selected, the right panel shows its drawings — combined, front, top, left and section views — for quick reference on the workshop floor.

Only views that show real features (cutouts, holes, bevels, non-rectangular profiles) are produced. If a particular view would just be a plain rectangle, it's skipped — the dimensions in the table already convey that. A part with no features at all gets no drawings.

For wood parts that aren't straight prisms (parts with cutouts, bevels or mitres), an extra **3D** button appears next to the drawing views. Clicking it opens the isolated part in an interactive 3D viewer, so any feature that's hard to read on a 2D drawing can be inspected directly. The button only shows up when this 3D model is available.

## Connection to Other Features

- Material requirements are derived from the designs and their BoM data.
- The [Delivery & Racks](/guide/logistics/delivery/) feature uses the logistics data to plan how completed assemblies are loaded for transport.
- [Reports](/guide/reports/) can generate Bills of Materials for ordering the materials tracked here.

pages.title: Delivery & Racks
pages.body:
# Delivery & Racks

The Delivery view is where you decide how finished panels will travel: you arrange them on racks,
and that arrangement drives the order the factory produces them in.

<!-- TODO: screenshot of the delivery view with a loaded A-frame rack -->

[[toc]]

## Delivery dates

A rack load has a **delivery date**: when it is due on site. Fill it in and the Delivery screen
sorts by it, soonest first, and marks anything past its date and not yet delivered as **Late**.

Leave it empty while the load is only a plan. An undated rack sorts last and is never late.

## When to use it

Rack planning happens **before** production, not after:

1. You arrange the racks the way the panels need to ship and be built on site.
2. That arrangement sets the production order.
3. The factory produces the panels.
4. Workers mark each panel as loaded on its rack as it comes off the line.

So the panels you are arranging have not been made yet. That is normal, and the view shows their
real status without treating "waiting" as a problem.

## Two things with two names

- A **rack setup** is a kind of rack your factory owns — an A-frame, a wall rack, a flat bed. You
  own several identical ones of each; the app does not track which physical unit gets used.
- A **rack load** is one rack filled with panels for one project.

## Rack setups

Manage them from **Rack setups** in the company section of the menu.

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| **Name** | What people call this kind of rack. |
| **Loading pattern** | A-frame (panels on both sides), single side, or flat bed. |
| **Usable length** | How long a row can be. Panels placed side by side have to fit in it. |
| **Stack depth per side** | How much thickness you can stack away from the frame. |
| **Max panel height** | The tallest panel the rack takes. |
| **Max overhang per end** | How far a row may stick out past each end of the rack. |
| **Strapped rows** | Which rows are tied to the frame. See below. |

The sizes are guides, not rules. The app warns when a load goes over them and lets you carry on.

When a rack goes out of service, **archive** it. It disappears from the dropdowns and every load
ever made with it keeps working. Deleting is only possible for a setup no load has ever used.

## Building a rack load

Press **New rack load**, or *Edit* on an existing one. The editor opens in three columns: load
details, panels to load, and the rack.

1. Pick the rack setup on the left. The capacity bars appear once it is set.
2. Filter the panel list in the middle by production line, phase, batch or scheduled date. Those
   fields are a filter, not part of the load — they sit in their own boxed **Filter the panels**
   block, with a **Clear** button and the count of what is left underneath.
3. Click a panel to put it on the rack.
4. Drag panels to reorder them. Drag two into the same row to place them side by side. Drag onto
   the strip marked `+` to start a new row.
5. Fill in the description, the location, the **delivery date** and, if you use it, a status, in
   the first column.
6. Press **Save load**.

Rows tied to the frame are marked with a padlock. Which ones those are comes from the rack setup —
see **Strapped rows** below.

### Reading the capacity bars

Each row has a bar showing how much of the rack length it uses, and each side shows how deep the
stack has got. Green is fine, amber is close or hanging over within the allowance, red is over.
Nothing is blocked: you decide what fits.

If a panel shows **Dimensions not measured**, its design has not been analysed yet, so the app is
drawing it at a placeholder size. Run the analysis to see the real one.

## Setting the production order

This is done where production order already lives: the **panel sorting dialog of a batch**.
There you get a **Sort by rack loading** button, which arranges the panels the way their racks
get loaded — load by load, and inside each one starting from the row against the frame. Each
panel also shows a small chip with its rack and its position on it, so you can check the order
against the plan before saving.

## The Delivery screen

Delivery is now a mode of its own, next to Logistics and Production. Pick it in the left menu and
you get the racks instead of the panels: a row per rack load with how far along it is, and the
rack itself when you tap one.

It is built for a tablet standing next to the rack. Everything is a button you can see — there are
no menus to open and nothing hidden behind a long press.

### The list

Three tiles at the top filter it: **All**, **To load** and **To deliver** — the two jobs a rack
still has left on it. Tap one to filter, tap it again to clear it.

Each row shows the rack's delivery date, its rack setup and its location, and a bar with where its
panels are: green for delivered, blue for in the rack, orange for still to load. The state is
written across the bar, with your own note in brackets after it. A rack past its delivery date shows
its date in red.

Pick **All projects** at the top and you get every rack the company owes anyone, soonest first,
grouped by project.

### Working a rack

Tap a rack to open it. You get the drawing, the panel list and the buttons.

**Each panel has its own three buttons: Not loaded, In rack, Delivered.** One tap sets the state.
Tap the wrong one and the button next to it puts it back — nothing asks you to confirm, because
nothing there needs undoing twice.

Tapping a panel in the drawing points at its row in the list. The drawing is the map; the list is
where you work.

Along the bottom, three buttons for the whole rack: **Unload all**, **Load all** and
**All delivered**. Only *Unload all* asks first — the other two are undone by the button next to
them in one tap. Managers also get **Edit**, to change the arrangement.

Printing the stickers stays in Reports, where it was: it is not something you do standing at a rack.

### Scanning

With a rack open, scanning a panel's QR marks that panel as in the rack instead of opening it —
which is what you want with the panel in your hands. Scan anything else, or scan with no rack open,
and nothing changes: it opens the panel as always.

## Marking panels as loaded

Once panels come off the line, mark them:

- **On the whole rack** — *Load all* or *All delivered* from the Delivery screen, or the same two
  from the load's card in the planning view. *Unload all* puts them all back.
- **One panel at a time** — the three buttons on its row in the Delivery screen, or the rack button
  in the [Viewer](/guide/viewer/).

This is what fills the delivery chart on the dashboard, so it is worth doing.

## Printing rack labels

Generate [Rack Load Stickers](/guide/reports/qr_stickers/) for a load. One rack per A4 sheet,
landscape. The QR takes the whole left half of the sheet, so it can be scanned from across the
workshop and at an angle. Beside it: the load name, the rack and its loading pattern, the
project, the client, the location, the drawing, and the panels in loading order with the
strapped rows marked.

The delivery date is printed large, above the project: it is what the driver looks for. A rack with
no date yet simply leaves it out.

Scanning the QR opens the rack on a phone or tablet, with the drawing, the panel list and the
buttons. Stickers printed before this change still work.

## Strapped rows

Some racks tie the first row down to the frame. Those panels are loaded first and come off last, and
the app marks them with a padlock everywhere they appear: in the editor, in the Delivery screen, in
the drawing and on the printed sticker.

Which rows are strapped is part of the **rack setup**, because it depends on the rack you own:

- **Flat bed** — nothing is strapped. There is no frame to tie anything to, so there is nothing to
  choose.
- **Single side** — the first row is strapped, or none.
- **A-frame** — **A0**, **B0**, both, or neither.

The little diagram in the rack setup form shows it as you pick: the strapped row turns blue and gets
the padlock, and the rack itself is the orange bar labelled **RACK**.

Existing rack setups keep marking their first row, which is what they did before this was a choice —
except flat beds, which now correctly mark nothing.

## Overhang

Panels sit **centred** on the rack, so a row wider than the rack sticks out at both ends by the
same amount. How far it may stick out is part of the rack setup: **Max overhang per end**.

The bar under each row tells you where you are — green while the row fits on the rack, amber
once it hangs over but stays within the allowance, and red when it goes past it. It still lets
you save: as with the other rack dimensions, it warns and you decide.

A setup with the overhang left at 0 behaves exactly as before: anything wider than the rack is
over capacity.

## The rack drawing

The same drawing appears wherever the load does — the card, the rack's page, the rack button in
the viewer, and the printed sticker. One band per row in loading order, panels at their real
sizes, the strapped row highlighted, and the frame where it physically sits.

Each panel is drawn as a cross-section: its width along the rack by its thickness into the
stack, with the height written on it. On screen it also shows the panel's priority within its
batch as `number/total`, and a chip once that panel is loaded or delivered.

Rows are centred and the frame is drawn at the rack's real length, so an overhang is visible
rather than implied; dashed guides mark where the rack ends.

It is drawn from the arrangement itself, so it is never out of date with what you saved.

pages.title: Stock & Products
pages.body:
# Stock & Products

The Stock & Products view lets you manage your material catalog — the materials, sizes, and products used across your projects.

<!-- TODO: screenshot of the stock products management view -->

[[toc]]

## Catalog Sections

The view contains five tables, each managing a different part of your material catalog:

### Materials

The base materials used in production (e.g., types of wood, metal, OSB, plasterboard). Each material entry defines a material type that can be referenced across projects.

### Plate Sizes

Dimensional variants for plate materials. Define the available widths and lengths for each plate material so that reports and logistics can filter by specific sizes.

### Profile Sizes

Dimensional variants for profile materials (structural elements like studs, beams). Define the cross-section dimensions available for each profile material.

### Product Plates

Pre-cut plate products used in assemblies. Each entry combines a material with a specific size and any additional specifications.

### Product Profiles

Pre-cut profile products used in assemblies. Each entry combines a material with a specific cross-section size.

## Managing Catalog Entries

For each table, you can:

- **Create** — Add a new entry with its name, dimensions, and specifications.
- **Edit** — Modify existing entries.
- **Delete** — Remove entries no longer in use.

::: warning
Deleting a material or size that is referenced by existing designs or reports may cause issues. Only remove entries that are no longer needed.
:::

## Connection to Other Features

- The material catalog feeds into [Logistics](/guide/logistics/) for tracking material availability.
- [Reports](/guide/reports/) use material and size data for Bills of Materials and filtering options.
- Machine file generation uses material properties to determine processing parameters.

pages.body:
# Integrations & Webhooks

Webhooks let an external system react to what happens in produuz.it. When an event you subscribed to occurs, produuz.it sends an HTTP `POST` to your URL with a JSON body you choose.

<!-- TODO: screenshot of the webhook configuration form -->

[[toc]]

## How webhooks work

1. You create a webhook in **Company → Automations → Webhooks**, picking the events it reacts to and the URL to call.
2. You pick which blocks of data go in the body (**Payload content**).
3. When one of those events happens, produuz.it builds the body and posts it to your URL.

**One webhook can hold several events.** If the same endpoint should hear about three of them, pick all three in the same webhook instead of creating three rows with the same URL, secret and headers. Every request carries `"event"`, so your endpoint always knows which one it is.

The number of webhooks you can have is limited by your licence, and the counter is shown above the table (`3/10 Webhooks`). It counts rows, not events, so grouping events into one webhook uses less of your licence.

### What your endpoint receives

- Method `POST`, header `Content-Type: application/json`.
- The body always contains `"event"` with the event name, plus whatever payload blocks you enabled.
- produuz.it waits up to 5 seconds to connect and 10 seconds for your answer.
- **Any `2xx` counts as delivered** — `200`, `201` if you create a row, `202` if you queue the work, `204` if you answer with nothing. A `3xx`, `4xx` or `5xx` is recorded as a failure.
- **There is no retry.** If your endpoint is down, times out or errors, that notification is lost and nothing is re-sent. Every attempt is recorded, so you can see it happened — see [Delivery log](#delivery-log).

Calls are made by a background worker, not by the request that raised the event, so a slow endpoint of yours never slows down the tablet on the shop floor. Two consequences for your side:

- Expect the call **a few seconds after** the event, not at the same instant.
- **Order is not guaranteed.** Two events raised close together can arrive in either order. Use the `timestamp` in `serialized_event` if the sequence matters to you.

## Events

| Event | Triggered when |
|-------|----------------|
| `constructible_start` | An operator starts a panel or module in the production viewer (the panel checklist is opened and production begins). |
| `constructible_ready` | A panel or module completes its last station, or is marked ready in bulk from the constructibles list. |
| `station_start` | An operator starts one station for a panel or module. Also raised for each earlier station that is filled in when a panel is started at a later station. |
| `station_ready` | An operator marks one station as finished for a panel or module. Also raised for each earlier station filled in the same way. |
| `part_batch_start` | A part batch is started in the logistics viewer. |
| `part_batch_ready` | A part batch is finished in the logistics viewer. |
| `report_deprecation` | A new IFC is detected for a design and its existing reports are marked obsolete. |
| `rack_load_ready` | Every panel of a rack load is marked *in rack*. |
| `rack_load_delivered` | Every panel of a rack load is marked *delivered*. |

`unknown` and `mounted` rack statuses raise nothing: the first is an undo, the second happens on site.

The station events are the loudest of the list: one per station and per panel, so a line with six stations sends six times what `constructible_ready` sends. Starting a panel at a later station also fills in the earlier ones, and each of those raises its own pair. Subscribe to them when you track station occupancy; use `constructible_start` and `constructible_ready` when you only track panels.

## Configuring a webhook

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Name** | Free text, up to 80 characters. Only used to recognise the row in the table. |
| **Events** | Which events trigger this webhook. Pick one or several. |
| **Fire on every production line** | Fires whatever the production line, including lines created later. Disables the list below. |
| **Production lines** | The production lines this webhook fires on. Select at least one: an empty list means the webhook never fires. |
| **Payload content** | Which blocks of data to include in the body. See [Payload content](#payload-content). |
| **Auth header type** | `None`, `Secret` or `Bearer`. Adds an `Authorization` header. |
| **Secret** | The token sent after the auth header type. Only shown when a type is selected. |
| **URL** | The endpoint that receives the `POST`. Must be `http://` or `https://`. |
| **Custom headers** | Extra HTTP headers, as name/value pairs. |
| **Custom payload fields** | Extra name/value pairs merged into the body. |

### Production lines

A webhook only fires on the production lines you select. Selecting none is not a shortcut for "all lines" — the webhook stays silent, and the form warns you about it.

If you want a webhook to fire everywhere, turn on **Fire on every production line**. That covers the lines you have today and any line you create later, so you do not have to come back and edit the webhook each time. With the switch off, a new production line is not added to your webhooks automatically: add it yourself to each webhook that should cover it.

Three events never belong to a production line: `report_deprecation`, `rack_load_ready` and `rack_load_delivered`. They reach every webhook subscribed to them, whatever lines it lists, and a webhook holding only those does not need a line at all — the form does not warn about it. An event on a batch with no line assigned is treated the same way.

## Payload content

**Payload content** is a multiple choice. Each option adds one block to the JSON body. By default only `serialized_event` is selected.

| Option | Adds |
|--------|------|
| `serialized_event` | The production event itself, merged at the top level of the body. |
| `serialized_station` | `production_station`: the station the event happened at. |
| `serialized_constructible` | `assembly` and/or `module`: the panel or module the event is about. |
| `serialized_part_batch` | `part_batch`: the batch, its session proof and the sizes it covers. |
| `serialized_project` | `project__details`: the project the event belongs to, with your own project number. |
| `employees__client_ids` | `employees__client_ids`: your own ids for the people the event belongs to. |
| `serialized_employees` | `employees__details`: the same people as full rows, with name and alias. |
| `nicelabel_print` | A NiceLabel print job, merged at the top level. See the [NiceLabel tutorial](/tutorials/nicelabel/). |

A block that cannot be built is simply left out — a station payload on an event with no station, for example. The request is still sent.

### `serialized_event`

The production event, merged at the top level. The account the event was posted from is deliberately not included.

```json
{
  "event": "station_ready",
  "uuid": "4b0a3f2e-6c1d-4a1f-9c2b-9f9b1f0f2a11",
  "timestamp": "2026-09-14T08:41:12.884Z",
  "project": "9d1e7b6a-2f44-4f0a-9a1c-1b2c3d4e5f60",
  "assembly": "e8f7e7f7-3b27-41e0-bb78-99eae64ba7cd",
  "module": null,
  "part_batch": null,
  "assembly_design": 45213,
  "module_design": null,
  "report": null,
  "employees": [312, 318],
  "employee_aliases": ["JAN", "PIET"],
  "meta": {
    "frontend_timestamp": "2026-09-14T08:41:12.640Z",
    "station_name": "Nailing",
    "station": "7a2c8e11-9d3b-4c22-8f1e-0b5a6d7c8e90"
  }
}
```

`employee_aliases` is a snapshot taken when the event was recorded, so renaming or removing someone later does not rewrite history. `employees` holds the matching account ids.

### `serialized_station`

Resolved from the station uuid in the event's `meta`, so it is only present on events that carry one: `station_start` and `station_ready`.

```json
{
  "production_station": {
    "name": "Nailing",
    "uuid": "7a2c8e11-9d3b-4c22-8f1e-0b5a6d7c8e90",
    "production_line_name": "Line 1",
    "production_line_uuid": "1c2d3e4f-5a6b-7c8d-9e0f-1a2b3c4d5e6f",
    "client_station_id": "ST-02"
  }
}
```

### `serialized_constructible`

Adds `assembly`, `module`, or both, depending on what the event points at. Both blocks have the same shape.

```json
{
  "assembly": {
    "uuid": "e8f7e7f7-3b27-41e0-bb78-99eae64ba7cd",
    "design_uuid": "db0cb2a6-8fbf-46ac-81f5-ece6faca584e",
    "design_name": "ML-0B-5",
    "status": "working",
    "scheduled_prod_date": "2026-09-15",
    "client_order_id": "1030622",
    "batch_uuid": "e8986e12-4454-4ae5-a40d-4929d6a5b789",
    "batch_name": "Batch 1",
    "phase": "Phase_1"
  }
}
```

### `serialized_part_batch`

Only present on `part_batch_start` and `part_batch_ready`. It carries the batch, the proof of the session (times, pauses, the parts marked ready, the material declared as returned) and the sizes the batch covers, so you never have to walk the parts yourself.

```json
{
  "part_batch": {
    "uuid": "b1f0c2d3-4e5f-6a7b-8c9d-0e1f2a3b4c5d",
    "name": "PB-2026-014",
    "status": "working",
    "priority": 0,
    "scheduled_prod_date": "2026-09-15",
    "production_line": "Saw line",
    "production_line_uuid": "1c2d3e4f-5a6b-7c8d-9e0f-1a2b3c4d5e6f",
    "project_name": "Vianen",
    "project_uuid": "9d1e7b6a-2f44-4f0a-9a1c-1b2c3d4e5f60",
    "parts_count": 412,
    "ready_count": 0,
    "sizes": [
      {
        "branch": "timber",
        "alike": "wood",
        "size": "38x140 C24",
        "size_uuid": "2b3c4d5e-6f70-4182-9394-a5b6c7d8e9f0",
        "erp_code": "W-38140-C24",
        "material": "C24",
        "finish": "planed",
        "parts_count": 240,
        "width": 38,
        "height": 140,
        "total_length_mm": 486200.0,
        "dims": [{ "dim": "38x140x2400", "count": 120 }]
      }
    ],
    "proof": {
      "uuid": "f0e1d2c3-b4a5-4968-8778-695a4b3c2d1e",
      "start_date": "2026-09-14T07:02:00Z",
      "ready_date": null,
      "paused": false,
      "elapsed_seconds": 5720,
      "worked_seconds": 4980,
      "user_name": "tablet_saw",
      "checklist": [],
      "materials": []
    }
  }
}
```

`alike` is the geometry family of the branch, taken from the project's IFC parsing setup: `wood` (measured by length), `plate` (measured by area) or `generic` (not measured). Profiles report `width`/`height`/`total_length_mm`, plates report `thickness`/`total_area_mm2`.

### `serialized_project`

The project the event belongs to. `serialized_event` already tells you *which* project by uuid; this block tells you which one it is **in your own books** — `project_number` and `client_name` are the fields to key on.

The key is `project__details`, not `project`, because `serialized_event` already uses `project` for the uuid.

```json
{
  "project__details": {
    "uuid": "9d1e7b6a-2f44-4f0a-9a1c-1b2c3d4e5f60",
    "name": "Vianen",
    "project_number": "5073H11L",
    "client_name": "Heijmans",
    "super_project": "",
    "start_date": "2026-09-01",
    "delivery_date": "2026-11-20",
    "archived": false
  }
}
```

The block is left out when the event has no project — a batch made without one, for example.

### `employees__client_ids`

The people the event belongs to, using **your** id for each of them — the `client_id` on their user account. When someone has no `client_id`, their produuz.it alias is sent instead, so the list always has one entry per person and stays aligned with `employee_aliases`.

```json
{ "employees__client_ids": ["EMP-0042", "PIET"] }
```

If you need to know for certain whether a value is your id or a fallback alias, use `serialized_employees` and read `client_id` explicitly.

### `serialized_employees`

The same people as full rows. The key is `employees__details`, not `employees`, because `serialized_event` already uses `employees` for the list of account ids.

```json
{
  "employees__details": [
    { "id": 312, "alias": "JAN", "name": "Jan de Vries", "client_id": "EMP-0042" },
    { "id": 318, "alias": "PIET", "name": "Piet Bakker", "client_id": "" }
  ]
}
```

### `nicelabel_print`

Builds a NiceLabel cloud print job from the panel the event is about and merges it at the top level of the body. Selecting it reveals three extra fields: **Printer**, **FilePath** and **API version** (`v1` or `v2`). Full walkthrough and example payloads in the [NiceLabel tutorial](/tutorials/nicelabel/).

## Events with a fixed payload

`report_deprecation`, `rack_load_ready` and `rack_load_delivered` are not production events, so **Payload content** does not apply to them. They always send their own block. Custom payload fields, headers and authentication work as usual.

### `report_deprecation`

```json
{
  "event": "report_deprecation",
  "design_name": "ML-0B-5",
  "design_uuid": "db0cb2a6-8fbf-46ac-81f5-ece6faca584e",
  "design_level": "assembly",
  "design_revision": 3,
  "project_uuid": "9d1e7b6a-2f44-4f0a-9a1c-1b2c3d4e5f60",
  "project_name": "Vianen",
  "affected_reports": [
    { "uuid": "c3d4e5f6-a7b8-4901-8234-56789abcdef0", "name": "Wood BoM", "document_type": "wood_bom" }
  ]
}
```

### `rack_load_ready` and `rack_load_delivered`

The load, the rack setup it uses and every panel on it with its place on the rack, under `rack_trace`.

```json
{
  "event": "rack_load_delivered",
  "rack_trace": {
    "uuid": "5f6a7b8c-9d0e-4f12-8345-6789abcdef01",
    "description": "Truck 2, morning",
    "location": "Yard A",
    "status": "loaded",
    "project_name": "Vianen",
    "project_uuid": "9d1e7b6a-2f44-4f0a-9a1c-1b2c3d4e5f60",
    "project_number": "5073",
    "rack_setup": {
      "uuid": "aabbccdd-1122-4334-8556-778899aabbcc",
      "name": "A-frame 6m",
      "type": "middle",
      "length": 6000,
      "width": 1200,
      "height": 3000
    },
    "panels": [
      {
        "uuid": "e8f7e7f7-3b27-41e0-bb78-99eae64ba7cd",
        "design_name": "ML-0B-5",
        "status": "ready",
        "delivery_status": "delivered",
        "client_order_id": "1030622",
        "batch_name": "Batch 1",
        "rack_side": "a",
        "rack_row": 2,
        "rack_row_pos": 1,
        "strapped_to_frame": false,
        "width": 3000,
        "height": 2800,
        "thickness": 300
      }
    ],
    "panels_count": 1
  }
}
```

`rack_side` is `a` or `b` — `a` is the only side of a single-sided rack. `status` on the load is a free-text note typed by the person who made it, not a computed state; the state you want is `delivery_status` on each panel.

A rack load spans whatever production lines its panels came from, so it is not line-specific: it reaches every webhook subscribed to the event.

## Delivery log

Every call is recorded: when it was made, which event it was about, the status code your endpoint returned, how long it took and, when it failed, the error.

The **Last delivery** column in the webhooks table shows when the webhook last fired, coloured by how that call went:

| | Meaning |
|---|---------|
| **Green** | The last call was accepted (any `2xx`). |
| **Red** | The last call was refused, errored, or got no answer at all. The tooltip says which. |
| **Grey** | Nothing has been sent yet. A webhook whose event has not happened is not a problem. |

The 🕘 button on the row opens the log itself: the last 20 calls with their status, duration and error. That is where to look when an integration stops working — a column of red rows with `ConnectTimeout` says your endpoint is unreachable, and a column of `401` says the secret no longer matches.

Some details worth knowing:

- Records are kept for **30 days** and then deleted. The log answers "what happened this week", not "what happened last quarter".
- **The request body is kept only for failed calls**, so you can see exactly what was being sent when it failed. A successful call keeps no copy.
- **Headers are never stored.** They carry your secret, and a log is read by more people than a settings form.

## Custom payload fields

Beyond the payload blocks, you can add your own name/value pairs, merged into the body of every request this webhook sends. Useful for constants your endpoint expects: a plant identifier, a routing key, an environment tag.

Each field has a **name** (the JSON key) and a **value** (a text string). If a custom field uses the same name as a standard field, **the standard field wins** and your value is dropped. Pick names that cannot collide.

## Authentication and headers

- **Auth header type** + **Secret** send `Authorization: <type> <secret>`, for example `Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...`. Choose `None` to send no `Authorization` header.
- **Custom headers** add any other header your endpoint requires, such as `Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key` for NiceLabel.

produuz.it does not sign the body. The secret is what proves the request came from your account, so use HTTPS.

## Use cases

- **ERP integration** — sync production status to your business system.
- **Label printing** — print a label when a panel starts (see the [NiceLabel tutorial](/tutorials/nicelabel/)).
- **Notifications** — send alerts to Slack, Teams or another messaging platform.
- **Logistics** — tell your transport system a rack load is ready to leave.
- **Quality tracking** — log production events in an external quality system.

pages.body:
# Account Settings

The Account page lets you manage your personal settings, security, and notification preferences.

<!-- TODO: screenshot of the account settings page -->

## Profile

Your account page shows:

- **Username** — Your login name.
- **Production line** — Your currently assigned production line.
- **Production station** — Your currently assigned station.
- **Language** — Interface language (if your admin has enabled multilanguage for your account).

## Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)

Enable 2FA to add an extra layer of security to your account. When enabled, you'll need to enter a one-time password (OTP) from your authenticator app each time you log in.

### Setting Up 2FA

1. Click **Enable 2FA** on the account page.
2. Scan the QR code with your authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Authy, etc.).
3. Enter the verification code to confirm setup.

### Disabling 2FA

Click **Disable 2FA** and confirm. You'll need to authenticate to complete the action.

## Notifications

Configure how you receive notifications from produuz.it:

- **Push / Browser notifications** — Receive real-time alerts in your browser.
- **Email notifications** — Get email updates for production events and webhook triggers.

Click the setup buttons to configure each notification channel.
